movements.name: Mustard
movements.note: This movement is the portrait before the story: where the title comes from, how your brain got wired sideways (Mr Strehler, St Kate's, the malaprops), the faith you were born into and hurt by and came back to, and the whole My Brain Is Mustard book you wrote instead of this one. Its spine is the 2026-06-06 passage: it starts with mustard, and every wound in the book will carry a nugget of something funny. What's strong is the voice material — the Kari-ism vignettes, the Aunt Gwen image, the Hoglunds routing story, the 'constant need to be smaller' confession — and the fact that the 2025-09-15 passage already names Chasing Chickens as the book that comes next. What's thin is scene: almost everything here is either a 55-word vignette or a dictated reflection, and the reader never gets one full, dated, on-the-ground scene of you being this person (a room, a day, a witness). Also note that the 2025-05-09 passage carries the entire 66-vignette compilation, including grief, Aldi, Spanx, weasel and cracked-plate pieces that belong to later movements; I've kept the 2025-05-09 passage whole here as the mustard book, but those vignettes will need lifting when the later movements are planned.
bigQuestions: There is no single full scene here of Kari today — the woman in long-term recovery, at 55, with the pugs, the granddaughters, the clients, the Mass music — that the mustard voice is speaking from. The reader needs one day in the present before the past starts.
The family roster is never laid out: your sister's name, your parents' names (or what you'll call them), Adam, Emily, Jakob, Nicole, the granddaughters — who gets named in this book and who doesn't?

The malaprops are presented as wiring, but the 2025-05-09 passage jokes about brain relapse and the 2026-01-14 passage mentions the bus crash — the reader will wonder whether the crash changed your language. Answer it once, early, in your own words: were you saying these things before the crash?
Sobriety date. Nowhere in this movement does the reader learn when you got sober or how long it's been — the mustard frame says 'in recovery' without a date to hang it on.

Chasing chickens itself: the 2026-08-05 passage says the title was never about 'play the tape forward' but about a chaotic quest to be who you were created to be — say in one voice memo what chasing chickens means to you today, so the title can be defined once in this movement and then earned.

chapters.title: I Am My Aunt Gwen
chapters.why: The title's earliest root is a four-year-old watching a farm woman do everything, so the movement opens where the chickens do.
questions: The 2025-05-31 passage calls her 'Aunt Gwen' and the 2026-08-05 passage calls her 'great aunt Gwen' — which is she, and on whose side (your mom's or your dad's)?
The 2025-05-31 passage says you honestly have no idea if the chicken memory is true — have you ever asked your sister, and what does she remember about that yard and that visit?
Where was Gwen's farm (town, state), and what was the last time you were there — how old were you?
The 2026-08-05 passage says the ladybug book is where you realized chasing chickens meant finding out who you were created to be — what is the ladybug book, and when did you write it?

chapters.title: Put That Book Down
chapters.why: Wee Kari before the trauma: the reader who hid behind a restaurant to finish a chapter, and the mother whose Christmas depended on a clean toilet.
questions: What was the book, what trip was this (which beach, what year, how old were you), and who was the one who said 'she even got lost on the beach' — your mom, your dad, your sister?
Give me one specific Christmas Eve, not the pattern — what year, which chore your mom named, what room you were in when she said Santa wasn't coming, and what happened next that night.

The 2025-12-24 passage says 'because my mom was crazy. I mean, not crazy' — what would you actually call it now, in one sentence, so this chapter doesn't have to explain her before the reader meets her?

The 2025-10-04 passage mentions your mom had you 'baptized' by an Indian woman when you were 4 or 5 and you thought the woman was dead when you first saw her — where was this, why did your mom do it, and what do you remember of the room?

The 2026-06-06 passage mentions your dad pushing you in the tire swing — where was that swing, how old were you, and is this the one tender memory of him you want standing before everything else he did?

I WASN’T LOST. I WAS READING.


They thought I was lost.
I wasn’t.
I sat behind the restaurant, reading.
Finishing the last chapter before 
“Put that book down!” resumed.
Thereafter I was the joke:
She even got lost on the beach.
I don’t even care. 
Sitting in the backseat, pretending to see the scenery,
I savored what came before The End

chapters.title: Mr Strehler and the No-Cliché Rule
chapters.why: Fourth grade is where the sideways language became a rule, and St Kate's is where it became a theory — this is the origin of the mustard brain as a craft, not a defect.
questions: What did Mr Strehler look like, what school was this, and what were two or three of his other chants and warnings besides the cliché one?

What was the St Kate's inter-departmental senior project actually titled, what year did you graduate, and which poet or poem was the spine of it — who taught you that it's up to the poet to tip language sideways?

The 2025-05-09 passage is a raw list of lines with no scene attached — who are the two or three people who hear these most (the ones who'd recognize them instantly), so the chapter can have witnesses instead of a list?

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard - Finalizing
passages.text:
weave what it takes from this with what you just had.. i like the new opening doloop but feel like there's stuff here to that needs to be there also : This is the part of the book where I’m supposed to explain myself. 
I get things wrong. I can’t use a cliché to save my life. 
There are reasons for this. In fourth grade, Mr Strehler taught me so much about language! I still remember his chants and warnings, one of which was to avoid cliché. If you’re not smart enough to say it in an original fashion, he admonished, don’t say it at all.
All righty then.
When I attended St Kate’s years later, my inter-departmental senior project was about language and how hard it is, in a world like ours, to make words mean. It’s up to the poet, I learned, to tip language sideways and force the reader to notice the words – and sometimes to wonder what they mean. 
So here goes:
My brain is mustard.
It’s not ketchup—people-pleasing and smooth. Nor is it mayo—mild and creamy.
It’s mustard. Spicy. Chunky. Unexpected. A little weird. Possibly expired. But it adds flavor—to everything it touches.
That’s me.
And this book? It’s the condiment tray of my life.
Every story in here is exactly 55 words. Not because I’m a minimalist (I am not), but because I love a good container.
Boundaries help me tell the truth without rambling into a metaphorical ditch (though I still take a few scenic routes, okay?).
Fifty-five words is just enough space to say something that matters—or something that shouldn’t matter but then you realize that it really does.
These stories were born in grocery stores and courtrooms, recovery meetings and kitchen disasters, heartbreaks and healing. They’re sacred and ridiculous and occasionally written during emotional turbulence. Some are straight up jokes. Others might punch you in the spleen.
But every single one is true. Even the ones about chickens.

chapters.title: Off the Top of My Butt
chapters.why: The Kari-isms in their vignette form — proof of the wiring in her own voice before the reader is asked to trust it through the trauma.
questions: The 2025-05-09 passage (Birthing Eggs) and the 2024-12-20 passage both point at the 'giving birth to an egg' line as the origin of the mustard idea — who is 'her' in that scene, where were you, and what was the emotional pain that was 'majestic'? the 2024-12-20 passage is dated December 2024; when did the egg line actually happen?

The 2024-12-20 passage's line about living with 40 women in a sober house and finding their lost fake lashes and snapped-off nail tips — is that Teen Challenge? Do you want it here as a wiring joke or saved for the movement where you're actually living there?

The 2025-05-09 passage (Crash Pig Dummy) is addressed to a friend who's been there for all the test drives — who is that, and are they the same person as the 'you' in the 2025-05-09 passage's Douse My Water?

The 2025-05-09 passage (Brain Relapse) says it's not early onset anything, just overthinking fatigue — did the bus crash leave you with any actual head injury or language change, and do you want the reader to know that before or after they laugh at the malaprops?

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard
passages.text:
THE AUDACITY


I woke up and chose violence.
By “violence,” I mean bold lipstick and an opinion.
People said, “You’ve changed.”
I said, “No, I just stopped asking permission.”
The audacity to exist loudly isn’t a flaw.
It’s a fruit of the Spirit.
Love, joy, peace... and audacity.
Blessed are the loud.
For they shall be heard.
 





WONDERMENT


I stare at the clouds like they’re my ancestors.
Gasp at frogs.
Touch tree bark like it owes me money.
Wonderment isn’t just for kids.
It’s for the tired. The heart-heavy. The nearly-but-not-yet hopeless.
Wonderment wakes you up.
Tells you life is still weird.
Still wild.
Still worth it.
Look at that squirrel.
Holy holy.
 





RELIGIOSITY IS NOT JESUS-APPROVED


Jesus never flexed a Sunday school sticker chart.
He flipped whole tables.
Ate with weirdos.
Loved the messy.
Religiosity makes rules; Jesus made room.
If your holiness is not rebellious, it’s not Him.
Stop handing out shame and calling it salvation.
He came for the ones in sandals and sarcasm.
And I qualify for both.
 





BIRTHING EGGS AND OTHER NONSENSE


The emotional pain was... majestic.
I looked her in the eye saying,
“I’m not giving in… 
I… I’m not giving birth to an egg over it!”
A moment of silence.
She blinked.
I blinked back.
Then we cackled like hens.
But that egg quote?
It’s what cracked open the joy.
Having a cow… overused, undercooked.
 





HIT BY A BUS, BUT A FANCY ONE


It’s a Tuesday.
I’m tired.
Mascara is a concept, not a reality.
But I brush my hair.
Throw on lipstick.
Look in the mirror and mutter,
“You look like you got hit by a bus... 
but like, a charter bus. With climate control.”
Then I laugh. It’s shaky.
Because honestly?
That’s high praise in recovery.
 





OFF THE TOP OF MY BUTT


People say “off the top of my head.”
Not me. I say “butt.” With gusto.
Because that’s where ideas live.
My best one-liners?
Butt-born.
My finest metaphors?
Butt-certified.
Call it divine inspiration or mustard splats.
Either way, when it hits, you better write it.
Some people think outside the box.
I think beneath the cheeks.

 





DOES MY BREATH SMELL LIKE COUGH? 


I meant to say I had a cough – I think.
Instead, I asked if my breath smelled like cough.
What is that actually?
I mean, how should you respond to the ridiculous?
I guess that is the power of a well-placed thought fragment.
And honestly, I may not always talk pretty.
But I talk memorable.











MY TOMBSTONE WILL SAY THIS


Here she lies.
She tried.
She cried.
She laughed until she peed.
She came up with that off the top of her butt.
She couldn’t stop.
Her tombstone?
Etched in Comic Sans.
With glitter.
QR code linked to her YouTube.
The message?
“She meant well. And she meant it loud.”
May she rest with snacks.
 





YOU'RE ALL BLURRY


I said it mid-conversation.
“I can’t hear you. You’re all blurry.”
They looked confused.
But I wasn’t wrong.
Some days people just… fuzz.
Words lose sharpness.
Faces static out.
It’s not ears or eyes.
It’s soul fatigue.
If I say you’re blurry, just shut, for God’s sake.
The world won’t fall apart.
But I could.


 





IF THE SHOE FITS, YOU MUST ACQUIT


What did I mean when I said, “If the shoe fits, you must acquit?”
It just flew out.
I think that’s what matters.
Sometimes I drop logic and pick up Dr. Seuss.
If it rhymes, it’s truth.
And if it doesn’t?
Well, then the shoe didn’t fit.
And the only thing to do is acquit.

 





A WEEK OF SUNDAYS


Too long. Too weird. Too much food and passive-aggressive weather.
That’s what it felt like.
A long week of Sundays.
Like one long awkward pause.
And laundry piled with existential dread.
But also pajamas.
Maybe pie.
There’s beauty in the weird.
Even when time turns stretchy.
Even when hope wears slippers and asks dumb questions.

 





BATTERING RAM BABY


She wanted in line first.
She had a stroller.
She weaponized the baby.
Bumped ankles.
Swung the diaper bag like Thor’s hammer.
I was all, “Look! She’s using her baby as a battering ram.”
I wasn’t wrong and no one disagreed.
Some moms carry snacks.
Others vengeance.
Maybe there’s some carrying respect.
But just—Ouch.

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard
passages.text:
HEAD SENSENESS


“I want someone who has head senseness,” I said.
They blinked.
I suppose I meant common sense.
Emotional regulation.
The ability to stay upright in crisis.
But “head senseness” felt more true.
It’s a vibe.
Rare.
You know it when you see it.
And you marry it when you’re lucky.
Or bribe it with lasagna.
 





LIKE AN ORCHID HOUSE


“I’m hot,” I said.
“Like an orchid house.”
Then I paused.
Because what does that even mean?
Too warm?
Too moist?
Too…fragrant?
Too much in general?
I don’t know.
But the imagery stuck.
Humidity plus drama plus exotic vibes.
That's me, baby.
Delicate but thriving in a glass box full of fog and questionable choices.
 





BRAIN RELAPSE


I forgot.
Again.
Whatever I was supposed to do—
Vanished.
Mid-thought.
I announced, “I had a brain relapse.”
Because that’s what it felt like.
Like my frontal lobe just packed a bag and left.
It’s not early onset anything.
It’s just overthinking fatigue.
Recovery includes the brain too, darling.
And also? Where are my pants?
 





ICEBERG POO


Someone said I was exaggerating.
I said, “I don’t just poo off the tip of an iceberg.”
Meaning: when I go, I go deep.
Barncle-deep. Echo-deep.
Don’t ask for surface-level drama and expect polite metaphors.
This isn’t Titanic Lite.
It’s Full Depth Emotional Release™, 
With weird grief-seahorses swimming laps around generational wounds.
Pack a snorkel.
 





ANNOYMENTS


Not appointments.
Not annoyances.
Annoyments.
It’s when you schedule your own misery.
Say yes when “heck no” is the holy answer.
Volunteer because you’re too Midwestern to decline.
Then dread it for days, while eating crackers in your car.
It's a trap.
So. Cancel with flair.
You’re allowed to change your mind.
And your shoes.
 





EGG ROLLS WITH PIZZA INSIDE


“I’m gonna make egg rolls with pizza in it,” I said.
Invented a cultural mashup instead.
Asian-Italian Midwest fusion.
Is it a snack?
A revolution?
An accident?
Yes.
But also a metaphor:
Sometimes life comes out weird,
but delicious.
Serve it anyway. With flair.
And put ranch on the side.
Or don’t. Sauce is extra.







YOU OLD DOO-HICKEY MOMMA


No idea where it came from: 
“You just suck it! Suck it doo-hickey momma!”
It leapt out. Mid-argument. Mid-laundry. Mid-something.
I said it with confidence, like a spiritual threat and a curse in one.
I don’t know what it meant, MEANT it.
Sometimes language isn’t logical.
It’s emotional jazz hands with a side of sass.
 





DOO HICKEY MOMMA, PART 2


I shouted it with glory:
“Suck it, suck it, Doo-Hickey Momma!”
Spur of the moment.
Zero context.
Maximum power.
It was part threat, part revival chant.
Made no sense.
But everyone heard me.
Sometimes a woman needs a phrase so confusing, it becomes sacred.
That one?
Is mine.
Tattoo it on my favorite soup pot.
 





YOU’RE TRYING TO DOUSE MY WATER


Why are you dousing my raging fire?
And also splashing my water.
I need that for emotional hydration.
You come at me with your logic bucket?
I don’t think so.
Let me simmer in my chaos broth.
It’s my puddle.
Let me be soggy in peace.
Stop dousing my water.
It’s sacred, and slightly tepid.

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard
passages.text:
UP YOUR BUTT WITH A RUBBER TRUCK


I swear we all said it in the 70s:
Up your butt with a rubber truck!
It’s not violent.
Just uncomfortable.
Said with exasperation.
Usually when someone’s losing the battle.
It’s a phrase from the sacred scrolls of Snark.
Translation:
Back off immediately.
Or I will park my entire mood in your orbit.
With tires.

 





THAT'S WHEN GOD ATTACKS! 


We were talking about divine timing.
Someone said, “He shows up when you least expect it.”
And I blurted, “That’s when God attacks!”
Laughter.
Silence.
A little fear.
But honestly?
Accurate.
Sometimes God comes in loud.
Wrecks your plans.
Throws glitter at your trauma.
Then hugs you.
All with a lesson you didn’t ask for.

 





FACE SIDE OF MY HEAD


I fell.
Said I hit the “face side of my head.”
Because there’s another side that’s also head but not face.
I wasn’t wrong.
Just overly descriptive.
Or I tipped language sideways.
The thing is—
Everyone knew my meaning which is the purpose of language.
I have a knack for weird phrasing with everlasting impact.

 





I WAS WALKING ON FOOT, AND…


“Well, I was walking on foot, and ...”
Of course I was.
After all, how else can we walk?
Was it for emphasis? 
Because there are days when moving at all feels miraculous.
When each step is rebellion.
I forget, sometimes, how words work.
Still, I stand by it.
I walk.
On foot.
With flair.

 





HOW HAPPY IS A CLAM? 


It sounds wrong.
Because it is.
But I said it.
“I’m as happy as a clam in a seafood diner.”
I expressing joy—or trying to.
Instead I suggested mollusks enjoying their own demise.
Honestly?
That’s accurate.
Happiness in chaos.
Peace in the boiling pot.
I am that clam.
Seasoned, confused, and somehow still grinning.

 





CRASH PIG DUMMY


I said it with gusto.
As usual.
“Sorry you’re always my crash pig dummy.”
Not quite the phrase.
But it hit.
You’ve been there for all my test drives through dysfunction.
The first to get whiplash when I try a new coping skill.
We’ve survived many emotional airbags, friend.
Still, it hasn’t been all pleasure.

 





THUNDERBOLT ATTACKS


You said something wild. Bold. Reckless.
I responded, “I’m surprised you didn’t get hit by a thunderbolt.”
I didn’t mean lightning bolt. 
Don’t judge my thunderbolt and make me call it lightning.
The God of the universe does all things.
He can throw any kind of bolts he chooses.
I mean what I say, dagnabit.


 





SHAPED UP THE SHIP. OR WHATEVER. 


I meant to say “shape up or ship out.”
Instead I said, “I’ve shipped up the shape.”
Or possibly, “shaped up the ship.”
Whatever.
The point is—
I made progress.
Rearranged the mess.
Put some bows on my baggage.
Is it perfect?
Nope.
But it floats.
And I’m captaining this disaster with coffee and charisma.








THAT’S MY BUTT, DON’T WEAR IT OUT


Someone made a joke at my expense.
I said, “That’s my butt, don’t wear it out.”
Felt poetic.
Rude but righteous.
I stand by it – or sit on it.
There’s only so much backside to go around.
You don’t get to borrow my dignity and call it comedy.
Touché, and also—
Back off my behind.
 





WALMARTS IN THE DUNE BUGGIES


“There aren’t any Walmarts in the cities,” I said in disgust.
“They’re only in the dune buggies.”
I know exactly what I meant: suburbs.
And it felt accurate.
Like a fever dream from a Midwest road trip.
I grew up in the burbs but won’t go back.
Though cheese curds are better outside city limits.





 





TEUTONIC PLAGUES RUBBING TOGETHER


“Earthquakes happen when two Teutonic plagues rub together,” I said.
And I meant plates.
But it was too late.
The phrase has now been born.
Somehow German medieval diseases are now shaking the ground.
And I?
I was goddess of the quirky science moment.
But also?
I really kind of like my version.
So there.

 





LET THE BEACH JUICE WASH OVER US


“Can we go to the lake and just let the beach juice wash over us?” I asked.
Meant sunshine. Damp breezes.
It’s reedom and fun, laden with salt and hope.
Laughter in waves and sticky sunscreen blessings.
Sometimes peace comes with goosebumps and grape soda.
Let the beach juice flow.
It’s baptism, but with snacks.

chapters.why: The wiring seen from outside: the boss who waits through seven redos, the cow with its cud, the radiance she keeps trying to shrink — this is who the world meets, and why the world sometimes doesn't like her.
questions: What was Hoglunds (a bus company?), what year was the routing story, what was your title there, and do you want the guy who drew the routes seven times named?

THE CHURCH HURT ME, TOO


I was born into that church.
Baptized, confirmed, married—betrayed.
She smiled in the pew while lying in my bed.
Pantyless psalmist.
You can’t make this stuff up.

In coffee-stained journals,
in recovery rooms,
in songs sung alone.
Holiness, unperformed.
Truth, uninvited—but finally free

The Opening Dollop
This isn’t a preface. It’s an opening splat. It’s a public remembering. 
I wrote this book because I finally remembered who I was made to be – and I’m doing it out loud, on paper, in full view of whoever might wander by. That’s the miracle and the mess of it: this isn’t polished testimony. This is mustard. It stains.
I do not write for approval, but I like it anyway.
I am not smoothing it so it goes down easy.
This isn’t ketchup. This isn’t mayo. This is me – sharp, weird, unexpected, often too much, sometimes expired, and somehow… still holy as cluck.
These stories? They’re little flashes of truth
They came out of recovery meetings, courtrooms, car rides, long silences, and late-night parking lot prayers. They’re stained with regret and glitter. Some are clearly miracles. Others are just well-timed jokes. 
I wrote 55 of them because I’m 55.
Because boundaries make my chaos feel safe.
Because exactly 55 words feels like the kind of container where I could stop explaining and just start telling the truth.
These vignettes are not all clean. They don’t wrap up nicely. Some of them contradict with each other – just like memories do. Just like healing does.
And still – they matter. 
Because they’re mine.
And I’m remembering myself in public now. 
Now with a whisper but with a full condiment splat.
If it gets on your pants? Good.
Maybe it was time for a new outfit anyway.
And listen. This writing exercise is helping me relinquish my strange fear of being vulnerable in print. It’s an awkward fear because I am called to tell the story of my recovery. Chasing Chickens: Through the Clucking Chaos comes next. You won’t want to miss it. \

My Brain Is Mustard: 55 Stories That Shouldn’t Work but Do
Hi. I’m Kari.
And this is the part of the book where I’m supposed to explain myself.
So here goes:
My brain is mustard.
Not ketchup—people-pleasing and smooth.
Not mayo—mild and creamy.
Mustard. Spicy. Chunky. Unexpected. A little weird. Possibly expired. But it adds flavor—to everything it touches. That’s me. And this book? It’s the condiment tray of my life.
Every story in here is exactly 55 words.
Not because I’m a minimalist (I am not), but because I love a good container. Boundaries help me tell the truth without rambling into a metaphorical ditch (though I still take a few scenic routes, okay?). Fifty-five words is just enough space to say something that matters—or something that shouldn’t matter but somehow really does.
These stories were born in grocery stores and courtrooms, recovery meetings and kitchen disasters, heartbreaks and healing. They’re sacred and ridiculous and occasionally written during emotional turbulence. Some are straight up jokes. Others might punch you in the spleen.
But every single one is true.
Even the ones about chickens.
I believe in the divine gift of laughter—especially in the midst of chaos. I believe humor is holy. I believe God meets us exactly where we are, even if where we are is face-down on the bathroom floor with one eyebrow and no clean forks. I believe grief and giggles can live in the same sentence.
So here you go.
Fifty-five little mustard packets of life.
Some shouldn’t work.
But somehow—they do.
Kind of like me.
Now read a few. Snort a little. Text your weirdest friend. Then write your own.
There’s room for all of it here.
And if it makes you laugh until you pee?
You’re welcome.
With love, joy, and a laminated binder tab for every emotion,
Kari Kounkel

passages.text:
these are the final 66... we need to whittle it down.. help me cut 11 with reasons.. : MY BRAIN IS MUSTARD


My brain is not mayo. 
No. It’s mustard.
Tangy.
Speckled with unprocessed tangents.
Useful in small doses.
Splats everywhere.
It sticks to things.
And stains a little.
People want answers—
I give them metaphorical sandwiches.
Hold the logic. Extra sass.
My mustard brain isn’t broken.
It’s gourmet.
Even if sometimes it gets on your pants.
 





FIFTY-FIVE STEPS

One for each year.
One for the regrets I buried.
One for the truths I told too late.
One for forgiveness I gave myself.
And one for you.
The one who left.
The one I carried.
Fifty-five steps forward.
Some days I crawl.
Some days I soar.
I never go back.
Not even to peek.
 





THE CHRONICLES OF DIVORCE CREAM

Churning grief into dairy:
Garden herbs, a healing balm—
Or a just a strange taste.
Basil ice cream? Not bad.
Sage and zucchini? A crime.
I didn’t know heartbreak was edible.
But I tried it with my people.
They refused…
While spooning pain into bowls.
Between mint delight and pumpkin disaster,
I started tasting hope.



 

 





GOSPEL GRANDMA STARTER PACK

I’ll give her a purse stuffed with fancy ladybugs.
Add a glittery rock and a verse about camels.
She’ll smile and me and ask for special things.
I might crochet her a hat shaped like a cinnamon roll.
My love is strangely wholehearted.
Or should I say wholeheartedly strange?
Either way, we’re all in now.
 





THE FAKE LAUGH THAT STUCK

I didn’t mean to laugh. 
It was polite. Sorta performative.
But the sound made her smile. 
And then she snorted.
I laughed again, for real this time.
We laughed until we cried.
I hadn’t laughed like that in years.
Now we are forever friends.
The fake laugh was just one thing.
But it changed everything.
 





I WASN’T LOST. I WAS READING.

They thought I was lost.
I wasn’t.
I sat behind the restaurant, reading.
Finishing the last chapter before 
“Put that book down!” resumed.
Thereafter I was the joke:
She even got lost on the beach.
I don’t even care. 
Sitting in the backseat, pretending to see the scenery,
I savored what came before The End. 





MY LOLLIES SEEM GAGGED

At 21, I was unstoppable.
At 31, scathingly brilliant.
At 41, hitting homeruns regularly.
But now?
It feels like my lollies are gagged.
Or I’m shouting underwater with jazz hands no one sees.
I didn’t get quieter.
The world stopped listening.
Too bad.
I’m still spewing my mustard - 
And sharing what wisdom I have.

 





THE 13TH CLUCK

13 is not unlucky. It’s undeniable.
Adam born: 11.13.91.
Emily born: 11.13.92.
Jakob born: 2.13.95.
Nicole married Jakob: 5.13.22.
God loves a baker’s dozen, no?
Twelve disciples—and Jesus.
Twelve tribes—and God.
Thirteen is divine math.
It’s the bonus, the blessing, the proof.
This number follows me.
Not superstition—
just a lovely sacred sequence.

 





FIRST VIEW


I thought my heart was already as big as it could be.
Then came these tiny girls who each look like their daddies…
And the whole universe cracked open.
It wasn’t a second chance.
It's a whole new world.
A softness I didn’t know I needed.
I fell in. And I haven’t climbed out since.
 





SIT IN THE WEIRD


I overthink.
Under-sleep.
And text you a paragraph with seven metaphors and a meme.
I say, “It’s not that deep.”
But it is.
It's also everything.
That’s how I’m built.
Cosmic and cracked.
Laughing at it all.
Sometimes crying between lines.
But listen.
Don’t try to fix me.
Just sit in the weird with me.
 





HOPE CHICKEN THIGHS


I don’t want lean protein.
You can have the chicken breasts.
Give me the thighs…
Brain-healing meat that tastes like a second chance.
Hope isn’t dry meat.
It's crispy skins and a side of buttered boundaries.
I fed myself well, finally.
Not with guilt.
With fuel for my soul.
Recovery is delicious.
Especially with mustard.
 





IF IT’S NOT FUNNY, IT’S NOT FINISHED


Here’s my rule:
If I can’t laugh yet, I’m not done healing.
It’ll come.
Like a punchline you didn’t see coming.
The moment grief turns ridiculous—
Holy ground.
Until then, I wait.
Plot.
Hold the silence.
Rehearse my joy in advance.
Polish the punchline.
Because when it flips?
Oh baby.
The laughter is freaking glorious.
 





SUCH A HAPPY SNORT


She snorted in group once.
Ugly laugh. Real laugh.
It cracked my grief open.
I was still detoxing from all the pretending.
And she seemed so unfiltered.
Unapologetic even.
She made recovery seem…attainable.
Even funny.
That day I stopped pretending the healing.
We finally laugh together.
A sisterhood of snorters.
Because God is so good.








I VACUUMED A FROG


I didn’t see it.
Just heard the thunk.
Paused. Frozen.
Too late.
The frog was in the Dyson.
It haunted me.
Not because it died—because it lived.
Two days later it hopped out and judged me.
Wet. Dusty. Alive. Confused AF.
I felt that.
I named him Jerry.
I don’t think he forgave me.
 





OCD, OMC, COD... WHAT IS IT??? 


I alphabetize trauma.
List my fears.
Re-label them for fun.
OCD? Maybe.
OMC? (Oh My Chaos.)
COD? (Chronically Overwhelmed, Darling.)
Whatever it is, it’s all mine.
And it’s organized.
Usually color-coded.
Mental health isn’t always clinical.
Sometimes it’s just diagnosing yourself using acronym roulette.
And I’m okay with that.
Mostly.
Unless you move my Post-its.
 





WHATEVER FLOATS YOUR GOAT


I mean, do whatever floats your goat.
It’s not a typo.
It’s a lifestyle.
Goats are unbothered.
Headbutty.
Confused and confident.
So whatever floats your goat?
Do exactly that.
Chase joy.
Climb on a roof.
Sleep.
Scream-bleat at the patriarchy.
I’m not here to judge your vessel.
I’m here to celebrate your barnyard buoyancy.
Baaa-rilliant.






HEAD SENSENESS


“I want someone who has head senseness,” I said.
They blinked.
I suppose I meant common sense.
Emotional regulation.
The ability to stay upright in crisis.
But “head senseness” felt more true.
It’s a vibe.
Rare.
You know it when you see it.
And you marry it when you’re lucky.
Or bribe it with lasagna.
 





LIKE AN ORCHID HOUSE


“I’m hot,” I said.
“Like an orchid house.”
Then I paused.
Because what does that even mean?
Too warm?
Too moist?
Too…fragrant?
Too much in general?
I don’t know.
But the imagery stuck.
Humidity plus drama plus exotic vibes.
That's me, baby.
Delicate but thriving in a glass box full of fog and questionable choices.
 





ICEBERG POO


Someone said I was exaggerating.
I said, “I don’t just poo off the tip of an iceberg.”
Meaning: when I go, I go deep.
Barncle-deep. Echo-deep.
Don’t ask for surface-level drama and expect polite metaphors.
This isn’t Titanic Lite.
It’s Full Depth Emotional Release™, 
With weird grief-seahorses swimming laps around generational wounds.
Pack a snorkel.
 





ANNOYMENTS


Not appointments.
Not annoyances.
Annoyments.
It’s when you schedule your own misery.
Say yes when “heck no” is the holy answer.
Volunteer because you’re too Midwestern to decline.
Then dread it for days, while eating crackers in your car.
It's a trap.
So. Cancel with flair.
You’re allowed to change your mind.
And your shoes.
 





EGG ROLLS WITH PIZZA INSIDE


“I’m gonna make egg rolls with pizza in it,” I said.
Invented a cultural mashup instead.
Asian-Italian Midwest fusion.
Is it a snack?
A revolution?
An accident?
Yes.
But also a metaphor:
Sometimes life comes out weird,
but delicious.
Serve it anyway. With flair.
And put ranch on the side.
Or don’t. Sauce is extra.







THE AUDACITY


I woke up and chose violence.
By “violence,” I mean bold lipstick and an opinion.
People said, “You’ve changed.”
I said, “No, I just stopped asking permission.”
The audacity to exist loudly isn’t a flaw.
It’s a fruit of the Spirit.
Love, joy, peace... and audacity.
Blessed are the loud.
For they shall be heard.
 





RELIGIOSITY IS NOT JESUS-APPROVED


Jesus never flexed a Sunday school sticker chart.
He flipped whole tables.
Ate with weirdos.
Loved the messy.
Religiosity makes rules; Jesus made room.
If your holiness is not rebellious, it’s not Him.
Stop handing out shame and calling it salvation.
He came for the ones in sandals and sarcasm.
And I qualify for both.
 





BIRTHING EGGS AND OTHER NONSENSE


The emotional pain was... majestic.
I looked her in the eye saying,
“I’m not giving in… 
I… I’m not giving birth to an egg over it!”
A moment of silence.
She blinked.
I blinked back.
Then we cackled like hens.
But that egg quote?
It’s what cracked open the joy.
Having a cow… overused, undercooked.
 





HIT BY A BUS, BUT A FANCY ONE


It’s a Tuesday.
I’m tired.
Mascara is a concept, not a reality.
But I brush my hair.
Throw on lipstick.
Look in the mirror and mutter,
“You look like you got hit by a bus... 
but like, a charter bus. With climate control.”
Then I laugh. It’s shaky.
Because honestly?
That’s high praise in recovery.
 





OFF THE TOP OF MY BUTT


People say “off the top of my head.”
Not me. I say “butt.” With gusto.
Because that’s where ideas live.
My best one-liners?
Butt-born.
My finest metaphors?
Butt-certified.
Call it divine inspiration or mustard splats.
Either way, when it hits, you better write it.
Some people think outside the box.
I think beneath the cheeks.

 





MY TOMBSTONE WILL SAY THIS


Here she lies.
She tried.
She cried.
She laughed until she peed.
She came up with that off the top of her butt.
She couldn’t stop.
Her tombstone?
Etched in Comic Sans.
With glitter.
QR code linked to her YouTube.
The message?
“She meant well. And she meant it loud.”
May she rest with snacks.
 





UP YOUR BUTT WITH A RUBBER TRUCK


I swear we all said it in the 70s:
Up your butt with a rubber truck!
It’s not violent.
Just uncomfortable.
Said with exasperation.
Usually when someone’s losing the battle.
It’s a phrase from the sacred scrolls of Snark.
Translation:
Back off immediately.
Or I will park my entire mood in your orbit.
With tires.

 





THAT'S WHEN GOD ATTACKS! 


We were talking about divine timing.
Someone said, “He shows up when you least expect it.”
And I blurted, “That’s when God attacks!”
Laughter.
Silence.
A little fear.
But honestly?
Accurate.
Sometimes God comes in loud.
Wrecks your plans.
Throws glitter at your trauma.
Then hugs you.
All with a lesson you didn’t ask for.

 





FACE SIDE OF MY HEAD


I fell.
Said I hit the “face side of my head.”
Because there’s another side that’s also head but not face.
I wasn’t wrong.
Just overly descriptive.
Or I tipped language sideways.
The thing is—
Everyone knew my meaning which is the purpose of language.
I have a knack for weird phrasing with everlasting impact.

 





WALMARTS IN THE DUNE BUGGIES


“There aren’t any Walmarts in the cities,” I said in disgust.
“They’re only in the dune buggies.”
I know exactly what I meant: suburbs.
And it felt accurate.
Like a fever dream from a Midwest road trip.
I grew up in the burbs but won’t go back.
Though cheese curds are better outside city limits.





 





BEACH JUICE 


“Can we go to the lake and just let the beach juice wash over us?” I asked.
Meant sunshine. Damp breezes.
It’s reedom and fun, laden with salt and hope.
Laughter in waves and sticky sunscreen blessings.
Sometimes peace comes with goosebumps and grape soda.
Let the beach juice flow.
It’s baptism, but with snacks.

 





WHITE CASTLE TOWER


“You sit there in your white castle tower,” I said.
Ivory, White Castle—same thing.
Either way, you’re judging me from above,
with fancy thoughts and greasy opinions.
Meanwhile, I’m down here making life work.
Pass the mustard.
And wipe that holiness off your face.
It’s dripping.
Just like your theology.

 





NOT A BREAKDOWN—JUST A PIVOT


I wasn’t spiraling.
I was twirling.
Recalculating.
Getting new WiFi from heaven.
People thought, “She’s losing it.”
But I wasn’t.
I was loosening it.
Unclenching.
Unscheduling.
Untangling spaghetti thoughts from my miracle map.
You say breakdown.
I say reboot.
Also?
Shenanigans are also holy.
So is dancing barefoot during lunch.
On a Tuesday.
With pugs.





THE DAY I SAID NO 


One day, I said no. 
Full stop.
My old self would’ve explained.
Justified.
Sent an apology hot dish.
New me?
Said “No thanks,” and went to Target.
Didn’t spiral.
Didn’t backpedal.
Just said no.
A soft one.
A kind one.
Like a velvet sword.
Still sharp.
Still sacred.
Still swinging in the name of peace.






MUST BE THURSDAY AGAIN


The feeling hit.
The chaos.
The momentum.
The rich clarity.
And I thought, “Yep. Must be Thursday.”
Because that’s how I time-travel now.
In focus blocks.
Three hours of living fire.
Followed by twenty minutes of pug-walking dissociation.
Structure doesn’t kill creativity.
It cradles it gently.
Thursday is my sacred altar.
And I come prepared.

 





JESUS KNOWS I SWEAR SOMETIMES


I love the Lord.
And I say “ass” sometimes.
I’m not rebellious to offend - 
I’m rebellious because I’m honest.
He’s not threatened by my sass.
He laughed first, 
Because even heaven needs spice.
So yes, I pray with a side of sarcasm.
And sometimes Jesus answers with a wink.
Usually after a long pause.

 





CHICKEN: 1. KARI: 0. 


I chased it for seven minutes.
Flip-flops slapping.
Cussing like a pirate at VBS.
The bird turned.
We locked eyes.
It blinked first, but I tripped over a rake and saw God.
The chicken walked away smug.
I ordered a rotisserie that night.
Call it closure.
Maybe karma.
Better yet, call it poultry-based revenge therapy.

 





WHISPERING THROUGH MASCARA


My prayers came choked.
Mascara-streaked.
Muttered in parking lots and bathroom stalls.
God didn’t mind.
He took the smeared confessions.
Made them holy.
I didn’t have to fold my hands.
Didn’t need a sanctuary.
Or music.
Or breath.
I just reached out and
He ran toward me.
Every time.
Even when I reeked of failure.

 





MY WORD’S BEEN THROUGH IT


Torn pages.
One coffee ring.
Sticky note with “WTF, LORD?” in all caps.
It’s held me together.
I’ve cried over it.
Wrestled it.
Ran away.
Came back.
It waited.
It's been a battle field.
It isn’t pristine.
Nor am I.
To say it’s ancient – is true. 
Mighty powerful too.
It's undone me more than once.






GRIEF MAKES YOU STUPID


I put deodorant on my toothbrush.
Twice.
Sat in the car wearing only one shoe.
I cried because the grapes were too round.
Grief rewires you.
Turns you into a punchline.
But you laugh because if you don’t, you dissolve.
So I laughed.
With snot.
With rage.
With gum in my hair.
It definitely counts.

 





THE FUNERAL FART


I didn’t mean to.
It was quiet. Reverent.
Until it wasn’t.
I bent over to hug Grandma and the sound escaped like a squeaky balloon at a baptism.
A small child laughed.
So did I.
Grief cracked open.
Laughter poured in.
I’m convinced heaven loves a good snort during sorrow.
God made butts, after all.



 





CRACKED PLATE THEOLOGY


I broke a plate when I sent him away.
Shattered it.
Kept the biggest piece.
I Sharpied, “Still useful” on it.
Because I am too.
It holds paper clips now.
Little things.
Like hope.
Redemption isn’t always stained glass.
Sometimes it’s duct-taped pottery and the reminder:
You don’t need to be whole to be holy.

 





THE RECOVERY HAIRCUT


We chopped it off.
All of it.
Looked like a feral hedgehog or something.
But I grinned.
For the first time in a while, the outside matched the chaos within.
The world hated it.
But my soul whispered, “You’re free.”
Freedom looks like bad bangs and no regrets.
I tipped the stylist $20.
Bless her.

 





LOSING IT IN ALDI


I saw their favorite cereal.
It cost $2.49.
But grief taxed it at $1,000 of emotion.
My knees gave out near the frozen peas.
People shopped, grabbing those important goods.
I couldn’t. 
I left the cart mid-aisle in mid-life,
Knowing everything was different.
Paradigms shifted.
And you know?
I did not want them to shift.

 





THE DAY I CRIED IN SPANX


Spanx are the new corsets.
So tight I couldn’t breathe.
Heartbroken and compressed.
Why did I think shapewear would help?
It couldn’t fix me.
I guess it held me together—literally
Someone said I looked "snatched."
I wept into my coffee and whispered,
“Lord, release me from polyester bondage.”
He didn’t.
But the wine did.

 





JESUS LOVES ME AND SO DO LEGGINGS


The jeans didn’t fit.
Again.
I blamed the dryer.
Then my stress.
Then the patriarchy.
Swore a little.
Then found my leggings.
They held me.
Like Jesus.
Forgiving. Soft.
Stretchy in all the right places.
I wore them to pray, wore them at court.
I think I’ll be buried in them.
And Jesus will understand.

 





HOT DISH AND OTHER GRIEF BOMBS


They brought food.
So many hot dishes.
I don’t even like tuna.
But I said thank you and cried over crunchy onions.
Grief turns every meal into communion.
Even when it's beige.
Especially when it’s beige.
I kept the Pyrex.
Still don’t know who owns it.
Somehow grief made us all family for a minute.

 





IT WASN’T WATERPROOF. NOR WAS I. 


The label lied.
It said “24-hour wear.”
It maybe lasted four.
Funeral.
Ugly tears.
I looked like a raccoon who had seen too much.
People said, “You’re so strong.”
I said thank you as my face melted.
Grief doesn’t care about brand names.
It just appears from nowhere.
Uninvited.
Unrelenting.
Like Aunt Ruth with opinions.

 





EMOTIONALLY SUPPORTIVE LIP BALM


I keep one in every room.
Car. Bra. Couch cushion.
Each one is a totem.
If I can find my lip balm, the world isn’t ending.
When I can’t…
Panic.
Doom.
It’s not about moisture.
It’s about control.
And you better believe I once cried because I lost the cherry one.
That one had memories.

 





MY TO-DO LIST NEEDS THERAPY


•	Cry.
•	Overthink.
•	Bake something weird.
•	Avoid texts.
•	Apologize.
•	Create an LLC.
•	Rename the LLC.
•	Spiral.
•	Clean my car with one Lysol wipe and regret.
•	Rise again.

My planner is a soap opera.
Somehow I’m still the main character.
And God?
He uses my inadvertent – and sometimes vertent – plot twists.
Because He knows what I meant.







I’M AWAY. LAUGHING. ON A FAST CAMEL. 


Not fast because I’m productive—fast because I’m panicked.
Camels don’t need water.
I forgot I did.
I ran on dry sarcasm and iced coffee.
Fast camel energy is not sustainable.
Eventually you spit.
Or trip.
Or collapse dramatically under the weight of all the crap.
Rest, you beautiful desert beast.
Your oasis is calling.

 





THE SNOTTY LITTLE BITCH LIST


Not all healing is noble.
Some of it is petty.
Like listing people who hurt you using glitter gel pens – and glee.
I tried burning it once.
The matches were wet.
I’m not sorry. 
I revisit to forgive, which is divine.
So is documentation.
Let the record show:
I healed.
But I have not forgotten.


 





THE ONE, THE WEASEL


Weasels slink.
Smile.
Sanctify themselves with charm.
She was my friend.
Until she was my replacement.
Until she weaponized empathy like a ninja in yoga pants.
Until her lies bought her glory.
Eventually weasels expose their teeth.
Today, I laugh.
A rodent is always a rodent.
I remade my henhouse.
And the rooster still roosters.

 





I AM THE SPREADSHEET NOW


I made an Excel workbook so detailed it got baptized.
Conditional formatting?  Therapeutic.
Pivot tables?  A spiritual practice.
I couldn’t fix people.
But I could organize the damage.
Rows of chaos turned into columns of clarity.
Honestly, there is no crying in spreadsheets.
Some women pray.
Some rage.
I Excel.
And that, too, is holy.



 





DON’T FEED THE SHAME LLAMAS


Shame llamas spit.
They judge.
They live in your brain and hum passive-aggressively.
Shame llamas show up when you're vulnerable.
They chew your confidence and leave droppings on your progress.
But guess what?               
You can shut the barn door.
Starve the shame.
Feed the truth.
Find a real living llama instead.
Those ones are healing.
 







GRAVY?  A COPING SKILL? IT SHOULD BE. 


Gravy helps.
Imagine a Thanksgiving meltdown.
Tears over the mashed potatoes.
Sobbing problems to the canned cranberry.
But then, a brief pause.
I ladled gravy over everything like it was holy.
It didn’t fix the tension.
But it baptized the carbs.
Sometimes carb-based acts are the best self-love.
You can judge me but I survived.



 





THE MOMENT I LET MYSELF BE HAPPY


I laughed aloud.
Not the guarded kind.
The ugly, snorty kind.
So surprising.
And completely foreign.
I didn’t chase it away.
Didn’t guilt myself back into sadness.
That moment wasn’t a betrayal of the pain.
It was proof I survived it.
Joy walked in unannounced.
And you know what I did?
I let her stay.








SOMETIMES YOU CRY IN GOOGLE DOCS 


I call it “emotional formatting.”
You type.
You delete. Aggressively.
You sob. Secretly.
You hit Ctrl+S and keep going.
Some people journal in peace.
I write rage sermons and grocery lists in the same doc.
Then title it: “Wednesday.”
Because healing doesn’t come in categories.
It comes in bullet points, bold font,
and unhinged honesty.
 





I LAUGHED SO HARD I PEED A LITTLE


It was a ridiculous goat video.
And maybe Amber snorted.
We laughed ourselves silly.
I think we peed a little. Didn’t care.
That laughter cracked me open in the best way.
Like a glow stick.
Joy oozed out.
I basked in it. Both of us did.
Sometimes the spirit moves your bladder.
Honestly? Thank God.



 





HOT MESS HYSTERICS AT WALGREENS


Dry shampoo.
Chocolate.
A pregnancy test for someone else.
Chips and Coke.
The cashier said, “Rough day?”
I laughed until I hiccupped.
Said, “You have no idea.”
Then knocked over a stand of lip gloss.
Nothing tragic.
Just creative chaos.
Sometimes the universe trips you gently.
And laughter catches you before the shame can speak.








GROUP LAUGHTER IS A WEAPON


We meant to be serious.
But someone mispronounced “existential.”
Then someone snorted.
Followed by a fart.
We fell apart. All of us.
Sobriety in giggle form.
Nothing heals like laughing with people who’ve seen the real you.
Your messiest self is invited back again.
The meeting didn’t stay on topic.
But it saved us anyway.



 





THE BINDER WAS NOT A HOBBY


They laughed at my binder.
All those tabs.
Labeled: Goals. Budget. Emotional Spiral. Death.
But I wasn’t being quirky.
I was building a fortress.
Each divider, a weapon.
Each post-it, a psalm.
When life falls apart, I don’t crumble—I laminate.
You can’t fight chaos with vibes.
You need a Sharpie and a three-hole punch.


 





MY THERAPIST LAUGHED, SO I WON


I said something unusually awkward – but real.
She tried staying neutral.
She failed. Spectacularly.
We laughed for five full minutes.
Tears-in-eyes, can’t-breathe, therapist-lost-control laughter.
That’s how I knew I was getting better.
Not because I cried less.
But because I remembered what was hilarious.
Even broken.
Especially broken.
I should charge her for that session.


 





CASSEROLE CATASTROPHE


She brought tuna casserole to my breakup.
I was moderately offended.
But then I dropped the pan.
The sound?
Perfect.
Like a cheesy thud from heaven.
We stared.
Then erupted.
Cried from laughing, not pain.
The carpet never recovered.
But I did.
Sometimes rock bottom is served with cream of mushroom soup.
And a snort.

 





MY BRAIN IS MUSTARD, THE FINALE


It’s not smooth.
It’s zesty.
Sometimes spicy.
Often expired.
You want a clear thought? Too bad.
Here’s a squiggle.
Here’s a memory from 1998.
My brain isn’t broken.
It’s condiment-based.
So when you ask what I was just thinking…
Just know it was weird.
It possibly made someone laugh-cry.
And that someone is likely me.

Collapsed onto the bed in defeat.
Mid-battle, I whispered,
“This is how we die. Bound by Levi’s. Unfulfilled.”

It wasn’t a launch.
It was a landing.
I panicked.
Yelled, “Houston, we have landed the plane!”
It made no actual sense.
But it felt true somehow.
We didn’t soar—we survived.
Skidded into success like an exhausted goose.
When you’re coming in hot, sometimes landing is the victory.
Even if your transmission is wrong.

These aren’t silly mistakes.
They’re linguistic miracles.
Blessed are the misquoted,
for they shall inherit thoughtful debate.
I’ve survived with malaprops and mangled idioms,
Turning nonsense into nuance - 
Where the sacred meets the scrambled.

Just say it wrong with confidence.
Then trademark it, wearing glitter.

next six:






SIT IN THE WEIRD


I overthink.
Under-sleep.
And text you a paragraph with seven metaphors and a meme.
I say, “It’s not that deep.”
But it is.
It's also everything.
That’s how I’m built.
Cosmic and cracked.
Laughing at it all.
Sometimes crying between lines.
But listen.
Don’t try to fix me.
Just sit in the weird with me.
 





THE BUTTERNUT INCIDENT


I thought I bought a spaghetti squash.
But it was a butternut.
Carved into it with righteous fury.
It didn’t string. It splintered.
I was so grievously angry.
Nothing was peeling right for me.
So I hurled it at the compost bin.
Missed.
It rolled under my car.
Stayed there three weeks.
Same, butternut. Same.
 





HOPE COMES IN CHICKEN THIGHS


I don’t want lean protein.
You can have the chicken breasts.
Give me the thighs…
Brain-healing meat that tastes like a second chance.
Hope isn’t dry meat.
It's crispy skins and a side of buttered boundaries.
I fed myself well, finally.
Not with guilt.
With fuel for my soul.
Recovery is delicious.
Especially with mustard.
 





IF IT’S NOT FUNNY, IT’S NOT FINISHED


Here’s my rule:
If I can’t laugh yet, I’m not done healing.
It’ll come.
Like a punchline you didn’t see coming.
The moment grief turns ridiculous—
Holy ground.
Until then, I wait.
Plot.
Hold the silence.
Rehearse my joy in advance.
Polish the punchline.
Because when it flips?
Oh baby.
The laughter is freaking glorious.
 





FAST CAMEL ENERGY


I called it Fast Camel Mode.
Not because I was efficient—because I was frantic.
Dry humor, dry shampoo, and zero water.
Still I galloped forward, chaos trailing like toilet paper on my sandal.
But I’m learning now:
Even camels drink eventually.
And the ones who laugh while hauling baggage?
Those are the sacred beasts.
 





SUCH A HAPPY SNORT


She snorted in group once.
Ugly laugh. Real laugh.
It cracked my grief open.
I was still detoxing from all the pretending.
And she seemed so unfiltered.
Unapologetic even.
She made recovery seem…attainable.
Even funny.
That day I stopped pretending the healing.
We finally laugh together.
A sisterhood of snorters.
Because God is so good.

keep these lovely pieces in mind when i ask you for the reflection spread redos

🍯Honey Mustard 
When someone chooses to stay present in the middle of our beautiful confusion, without trying to sanitize or simplify it, something sacred happens. That moment becomes a sanctuary. The awkwardness becomes incense. The weird becomes welcome.
And maybe that’s the deepest form of friendship — not someone who explains you to the world, but someone who plops down next to you in the unexplainable and says, “Scooch over. I brought snacks.”

🌶️Spicy Mustard 
Don’t tell me it’s “not that deep.” I’ve got trauma with cliff notes and joy that requires a color-coded chart. I’ve felt whole galaxies inside a single song lyric and grieved the loss of a vibe. I am not a quick read. I am a scavenger hunt with bad lighting and too many tabs open.
You think I’m dramatic? Maybe. But dramatic people are the reason we have musicals and revolutions.

Then came these tiny girls who each look like their daddies…
And the whole universe cracked open.
It wasn’t a second chance.
It's a whole new world.
A softness I didn’t know I needed.

The moment grief turns ridiculous—
Holy ground.
Until then, I wait.
Plot.
Hold the silence.
Rehearse my joy in advance.
Polish the punchline.
Because when it flips?
Oh baby.
The laughter is freaking glorious.

•	Meeting someone who changed everything
•	Giving birth (to child or to an idea)
•	Saying “I’m done” and meaning it

alternates.text:
SUCH A HAPPY SNORT


She snorted in group once.
Ugly laugh. Real laugh.
It cracked my grief open.
I was still detoxing from all the pretending.
And she seemed so unfiltered.
Unapologetic even.
She made recovery seem…attainable.
Even funny.
That day I stopped pretending the healing.
We finally laugh together.
A sisterhood of snorters.
Because God is so good.








I VACUUMED A FROG


I didn’t see it.
Just heard the thunk.
Paused. Frozen.
Too late.
The frog was in the Dyson.
It haunted me.
Not because it died—because it lived.
Two days later it hopped out and judged me.
Wet. Dusty. Alive. Confused AF.
I felt that.
I named him Jerry.
I don’t think he forgave me.
 





OCD, OMC, COD... WHAT IS IT??? 


I alphabetize trauma.
List my fears.
Re-label them for fun.
OCD? Maybe.
OMC? (Oh My Chaos.)
COD? (Chronically Overwhelmed, Darling.)
Whatever it is, it’s all mine.
And it’s organized.
Usually color-coded.
Mental health isn’t always clinical.
Sometimes it’s just diagnosing yourself using acronym roulette.
And I’m okay with that.
Mostly.
Unless you move my Post-its.
 





HEAD SENSENESS


“I want someone who has head senseness,” I said.
They blinked.
I suppose I meant common sense.
Emotional regulation.
The ability to stay upright in crisis.
But “head senseness” felt more true.
It’s a vibe.
Rare.
You know it when you see it.
And you marry it when you’re lucky.
Or bribe it with lasagna.
 





ICEBERG POO


Someone said I was exaggerating.
I said, “I don’t just poo off the tip of an iceberg.”
Meaning: when I go, I go deep.
Barncle-deep. Echo-deep.
Don’t ask for surface-level drama and expect polite metaphors.
This isn’t Titanic Lite.
It’s Full Depth Emotional Release™, 
With weird grief-seahorses swimming laps around generational wounds.
Pack a snorkel.
 
Squeeze Packs: Spicy Splatters
•	A fake laugh turned real
•	When church stopped feeling holy
•	Your weirdest Google search
•	A food you now love that you once hated (or vice versa)
•	The feeling of finishing a big project

alternates.text:
ANNOYMENTS


Not appointments.
Not annoyances.
Annoyments.
It’s when you schedule your own misery.
Say yes when “heck no” is the holy answer.
Volunteer because you’re too Midwestern to decline.
Then dread it for days, while eating crackers in your car.
It's a trap.
So. Cancel with flair.
You’re allowed to change your mind.
And your shoes.
 





THE AUDACITY


I woke up and chose violence.
By “violence,” I mean bold lipstick and an opinion.
People said, “You’ve changed.”
I said, “No, I just stopped asking permission.”
The audacity to exist loudly isn’t a flaw.
It’s a fruit of the Spirit.
Love, joy, peace... and audacity.
Blessed are the loud.
For they shall be heard.
 





RELIGIOSITY IS NOT JESUS-APPROVED


Jesus never flexed a Sunday school sticker chart.
He flipped whole tables.
Ate with weirdos.
Loved the messy.
Religiosity makes rules; Jesus made room.
If your holiness is not rebellious, it’s not Him.
Stop handing out shame and calling it salvation.
He came for the ones in sandals and sarcasm.
And I qualify for both.
 





BIRTHING EGGS AND OTHER NONSENSE


The emotional pain was... majestic.
I looked her in the eye saying,
“I’m not giving in… 
I… I’m not giving birth to an egg over it!”
A moment of silence.
She blinked.
I blinked back.
Then we cackled like hens.
But that egg quote?
It’s what cracked open the joy.
Having a cow… overused, undercooked.
 





HIT BY A BUS, BUT A FANCY ONE


It’s a Tuesday.
I’m tired.
Mascara is a concept, not a reality.
But I brush my hair.
Throw on lipstick.
Look in the mirror and mutter,
“You look like you got hit by a bus... 
but like, a charter bus. With climate control.”
Then I laugh. It’s shaky.
Because honestly?
That’s high praise in recovery.
 
Squeeze Packs: Zesty Life Lessons
•	When you stood up for yourself
•	Your most unexpected “yes”
•	A betrayal that wrecked you
•	A comeback you’re proud of
•	A day you were breathtakingly kind
 





MY TOMBSTONE WILL SAY THIS


Here she lies.
She tried.
She cried.
She laughed until she peed.
She came up with that off the top of her butt.
She couldn’t stop.
Her tombstone?
Etched in Comic Sans.
With glitter.
QR code linked to her YouTube.
The message?
“She meant well. And she meant it loud.”
May she rest with snacks.
 





UP YOUR BUTT WITH A RUBBER TRUCK


I swear we all said it in the 70s:
Up your butt with a rubber truck!
It’s not violent.
Just uncomfortable.
Said with exasperation.
Usually when someone’s losing the battle.
It’s a phrase from the sacred scrolls of Snark.
Translation:
Back off immediately.
Or I will park my entire mood in your orbit.
With tires.

 





THAT'S WHEN GOD ATTACKS! 


We were talking about divine timing.
Someone said, “He shows up when you least expect it.”
And I blurted, “That’s when God attacks!”
Laughter.
Silence.
A little fear.
But honestly?
Accurate.
Sometimes God comes in loud.
Wrecks your plans.
Throws glitter at your trauma.
Then hugs you.
All with a lesson you didn’t ask for.

 





WALMARTS IN THE DUNE BUGGIES


“There aren’t any Walmarts in the cities,” I said in disgust.
“They’re only in the dune buggies.”
I know exactly what I meant: suburbs.
And it felt accurate.
Like a fever dream from a Midwest road trip.
I grew up in the burbs but won’t go back.
Though cheese curds are better outside city limits.





 





BEACH JUICE 


“Can we go to the lake and just let the beach juice wash over us?” I asked.
Meant sunshine. Damp breezes.
It’s reedom and fun, laden with salt and hope.
Laughter in waves and sticky sunscreen blessings.
Sometimes peace comes with goosebumps and grape soda.
Let the beach juice flow.
It’s baptism, but with snacks.

 
Squeeze Packs: Dijon Diaries
•	One ridiculous fight you started
•	Your kids’ biggest lesson to you
•	Falling in love with yourself
•	A moment of deep embarrassment
•	Something your body taught you

alternates.text:
NOT A BREAKDOWN—JUST A PIVOT


I wasn’t spiraling.
I was twirling.
Recalculating.
Getting new WiFi from heaven.
People thought, “She’s losing it.”
But I wasn’t.
I was loosening it.
Unclenching.
Unscheduling.
Untangling spaghetti thoughts from my miracle map.
You say breakdown.
I say reboot.
Also?
Shenanigans are also holy.
So is dancing barefoot during lunch.
On a Tuesday.
With pugs.





THE DAY I SAID NO 


One day, I said no. 
Full stop.
My old self would’ve explained.
Justified.
Sent an apology hot dish.
New me?
Said “No thanks,” and went to Target.
Didn’t spiral.
Didn’t backpedal.
Just said no.
A soft one.
A kind one.
Like a velvet sword.
Still sharp.
Still sacred.
Still swinging in the name of peace.






MUST BE THURSDAY AGAIN


The feeling hit.
The chaos.
The momentum.
The rich clarity.
And I thought, “Yep. Must be Thursday.”
Because that’s how I time-travel now.
In focus blocks.
Three hours of living fire.
Followed by twenty minutes of pug-walking dissociation.
Structure doesn’t kill creativity.
It cradles it gently.
Thursday is my sacred altar.
And I come prepared.

 





JESUS KNOWS I SWEAR SOMETIMES


I love the Lord.
And I say “ass” sometimes.
I’m not rebellious to offend - 
I’m rebellious because I’m honest.
He’s not threatened by my sass.
He laughed first, 
Because even heaven needs spice.
So yes, I pray with a side of sarcasm.
And sometimes Jesus answers with a wink.
Usually after a long pause.

 





WHISPERING THROUGH MASCARA


My prayers came choked.
Mascara-streaked.
Muttered in parking lots and bathroom stalls.
God didn’t mind.
He took the smeared confessions.
Made them holy.
I didn’t have to fold my hands.
Didn’t need a sanctuary.
Or music.
Or breath.
I just reached out and
He ran toward me.
Every time.
Even when I reeked of failure.

 
Squeeze Packs: Tangy Times
•	When someone underestimated you
•	A boss moment that needs to be remembered
•	Being dead wrong
•	What you didn’t say but should have
•	What you did say and wish you hadn’t
 





MY WORD’S BEEN THROUGH IT


Torn pages.
One coffee ring.
Sticky note with “WTF, LORD?” in all caps.
It’s held me together.
I’ve cried over it.
Wrestled it.
Ran away.
Came back.
It waited.
It's been a battle field.
It isn’t pristine.
Nor am I.
To say it’s ancient – is true. 
Mighty powerful too.
It's undone me more than once.






GRIEF MAKES YOU STUPID


I put deodorant on my toothbrush.
Twice.
Sat in the car wearing only one shoe.
I cried because the grapes were too round.
Grief rewires you.
Turns you into a punchline.
But you laugh because if you don’t, you dissolve.
So I laughed.
With snot.
With rage.
With gum in my hair.
It definitely counts.

 





THE FUNERAL FART


I didn’t mean to.
It was quiet. Reverent.
Until it wasn’t.
I bent over to hug Grandma and the sound escaped like a squeaky balloon at a baptism.
A small child laughed.
So did I.
Grief cracked open.
Laughter poured in.
I’m convinced heaven loves a good snort during sorrow.
God made butts, after all.



 





CRACKED PLATE THEOLOGY


I broke a plate when I sent him away.
Shattered it.
Kept the biggest piece.
I Sharpied, “Still useful” on it.
Because I am too.
It holds paper clips now.
Little things.
Like hope.
Redemption isn’t always stained glass.
Sometimes it’s duct-taped pottery and the reminder:
You don’t need to be whole to be holy.

 





THE RECOVERY HAIRCUT


We chopped it off.
All of it.
Looked like a feral hedgehog or something.
But I grinned.
For the first time in a while, the outside matched the chaos within.
The world hated it.
But my soul whispered, “You’re free.”
Freedom looks like bad bangs and no regrets.
I tipped the stylist $20.
Bless her.

 
Squeeze Packs: Mustardy Memory
•	When you were the villain
•	A letter you’ll never send
•	A prayer you whispered
•	A boundary you didn’t know you needed
•	A smell that broke your heart

passages.chat: ChatGPT · Weird Gospel Analysis
passages.text:
CHAPTER 4
On Mustard Seeds and Mustard Brains
Matthew 13 — the mustard seed

4:1 The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, they say. The smallest of all seeds, growing into the largest of trees.
4:2 But let me tell you about Granny Bubblz.
4:3 There was a granny who wore bubbles and a pink cape, and the world told her grandmothers should be sensible.
4:4 Quiet. Dignified. Content to bake cookies and sit in rocking chairs and wait for visits.
4:5 But Granny Bubblz had a mustard brain. Which is to say, she couldn't sit still if heaven itself asked her to.
4:6 She had thirteen books to write. Felt playbooks to sew. Monthly letters to send. Baby Ninjas to train.
4:7 The world said, "Pick one thing. You're a grandmother now. Calm down."
4:8 But mustard doesn't calm down. Mustard spreads.
4:9 So Granny Bubblz built an entire universe out of bubbles and theology. A multimedia keepsake project that would take years to complete.
4:10 People asked, "Isn't this too much? Don't you want to just enjoy your grandchildren?"
4:11 And she said, "I am enjoying them. By building them a gospel they can hold in their hands."
4:12 Because here's what Granny Bubblz knew that the world didn't: love spreads sideways.
4:13 Holy isn't nice. It doesn't hand you a single lane and call it legacy.
4:14 It hands you bubbles and Baby Ninjas and thirteen books and says, "Build something ridiculous. Make it sacred."
4:15 So Granny Bubblz didn't prune herself. She let the mustard do what mustard does.
4:16 She wrote books about chickens and chaos. She sewed felt playbooks so toddlers could touch theology. She recorded videos in a tiara because joy is defiance.
4:17 And the seventeen tabs? They stayed open. Not as distraction, but as distributed threat assessment. As the way she'd learned to hold everything without letting anything fall.
4:18 Her brain worked seventeen directions at once, and people called it ADHD when it was actually anointing.
4:19 Because Granny Bubblz wasn't scattered. She was expansive.
4:20 She saw connections no one else saw. Built empires out of marbles and metaphor. Created legacy out of what the world called chaos.
4:21 And her granddaughters? They got a superhero who's also a prophet. Who taught them that the kingdom grows sideways, into cracks you didn't know existed.
4:22 Here is what they don't tell you about mustard seeds: they're invasive by design.
4:23 Plant one, and it takes over the garden. Refuses to stay contained. Spreads beyond every boundary you set.
4:24 Which is exactly the point.
4:25 The kingdom of heaven is not tidy. It does not stay where you plant it. It grows into places that weren't expecting beauty and calls it abundant.
4:26 So when they tell you to focus, to calm down, to pick one thing and do it well, remember Granny Bubblz.
4:27 Who wore a cape and built theology out of felt and refused to believe that grandmothers should be quiet.
4:28 Your mustard brain is not the problem. It's the garden.
4:29 Let it spread. Let it take over. Let Granny Bubblz teach Baby Ninjas that holy doesn't fit in a single row.
4:30 The world will call it chaos. God calls it kingdom.

movements.name: The Pile-On
movements.note: This movement is the weight that got stacked on you before the first drink: a mother who made your existence feel ridiculous, a father who couldn't stand your ideas outrunning his, and Joe, who took the basement and never gave it back. Its spine is the premise you stated in the 2026-06-06 passage and the 2026-06-06 passage — a gifted, kind, joyful kid shaped by wounded people until she read her own gift as a defect. The Joe material is the strongest thing here (the basement, Mary's 'whore in the bedroom', Shelley's twice-a-month, the driver-meeting hug, Pete's email) and the Malibus scene is a complete short story on its own. The mother is thin: one Christmas scene and a lot of naming her without showing her, and childhood itself (school, the piano, the 'gifted' part) barely appears. Several passages (the 2025-05-05 passage, the 2026-05-12 passage, the 2026-06-06 passage, the 2026-06-06 passage, the 2026-01-14 passage) ramble forward into the drinking years and Teen Challenge — I've marked PART on those so only the pile-on section comes here; the rest is already waiting for the later movements.
bigQuestions: There is no scene of you as a child being the gifted, joyful kid — only adults telling us you were. What is one moment, before Joe, when the 'center nobody could touch' was visibly there — the piano, a report card, a joke that landed?

Your mother is named as the first and deepest layer but appears in exactly one scene. What did she look like on a normal day, what was her voice like, and what was she like when she was drinking or using?
The reader will need the house: where you grew up, the bus company as a physical place, when the family business and your parents' divorce happened on the calendar. None of that is here.
Joe's father's porn addiction is mentioned as the root of Joe's — did you ever see it, and did Mary know? The movement implies a generational chain but never shows the link.

Between the basement (~1986) and the driver meeting there must have been years where it looked fine from outside — church, piano, the 'bus safety lady' — what did a good week with Joe look like in the early 90s, so the reader believes you stayed?

movements.name: The Chickens
movements.note: This movement is the long middle: thirty years with Joe, thirty-five at the bus company and the church piano, the boys, Pete, Salt, and the slow arrival of the question 'for what?' Its spine is the thing you say straight out in the 2026-06-06 passage — you made everything good, and it was still empty — and the reader has to watch you build every one of those good things (Adam's fist, the Thursday-night practices, the routing lessons, the eighteen-song concert) before it can land. The strongest material is anything with a room in it: the hospital bed with payroll, the counter with baby Adam, the hands coming up off the keyboard, dad tossing eight Malibu loan docs on the desk. What is thin is Joe himself in the good years (he appears mostly as the possessive boyfriend, the ESPN voice, and the man who cut the curls) and the 1997 bus crash, which is named three times as a hinge for your body and your weight but never once told. The Becca material is rich but arrives in four separate tellings, so the plan below splits it into the friendship, the fracture, and the last perfect song.
bigQuestions: The 1997 bus crash is the hinge of this whole movement — your body, your weight, the surgery — and it is never told. What happened that day?

Joe in the good years is almost absent: the reader sees the possessive first boyfriend, the ESPN voice, the porn head, the curls. Is there one ordinary good day with Joe — a baseball trip, a coaching night, something he did for the boys — that you can tell straight, without the ending in it?
Salt's music is described but never heard. Can you name the original songs you wrote for Salt, and tell where one of them came from?
Thirty-five years at the piano at church: when did you start (age 13, per Father Harry's 'first time Kari played'), and what was the first Mass you ever played?
The drinking starts somewhere in this movement ('the year Adam graduated,' 'it was kinda started before that') but there is no first scene of it. When did you first drink alone, and where?

It's a gorgeous little oasis.  Felt like we were in a different world.

We'd just started paddling when an odd thing happen.  A Very Angry Man started screaming obscenities at us.  At first I thought it was a tasteless joke.  It wasn't.  He was enraged.  He was throwing his arms around and pacing in and out of the lake with his boots on.

So apparently we were kayaking in "his" fishing spot. 

Weird.  The sign right behind him said "Public Access" and we were in a public park.

And, according to the Very Angry Man, we shouldn't even have boats if we are going to stay that close to the shore.

Weirder.  No one explained that "rule" to me in the past and I sort of thought kayaks were made for shallow water explores.

Also.  That Very Angry Man shouted Very Nasty Words in a Very Obnoxious, Loud Voice.

Weirdest.  I haven't been called things like that in my entire life.

I understand why people get charged with a crime - Assault - when they treat someone like that Very Angry Man treated us.  It was vile.

It didn't ruin the day.

Leave it to this Anti-Athlete to fugetaboutit and enjoy the day.

Well except when C dragged her paddle across the sand and I thought it was the beginning of the attack of the Mysterious Sand Creatures.

movements.name: The Breaking
movements.note: This movement holds the collapse: Salt and the friendship with Becca, the 13 Intrepids, San Francisco, the affair, the June 2014 DWI and Hennepin County, the van in Chinatown, the 3 a.m. WhatsApp text and the choking, dad's office and the floor, the annulment letter and the field, and the long drinking years after. Its spine is not the divorce — you said it yourself in the 2026-06-06 passage: the betrayal by the friend you told your whole story to is the wound, and every scene here either builds that friendship or shows it being used against you. The strongest material is the January 2026 dictation run (the 2026-01-14 passage–the 2026-01-14 passage, the 2026-01-14 passage–the 2026-01-14 passage): raw, dated, physical, and funny in the middle of horror — that run is most of this movement's keepers. What's thin: the year you kept the house, the divorce itself, the 2015–2021 drinking years (treatments, Dave, friends leaving), and anything about dating — you listed 'friends leaving, lectern, sex toys, dating' as belonging here, and only the sex toys are on the page.
bigQuestions: You said this movement includes 'friends leaving, lectern, sex toys, dating.' Only the sex toys are on the page. Which friends left, and how (one at a time, or all at once after Becca's campaign)? What is the lectern story? And what did dating look like in the drinking years — Dave, Michael, David are named in the 2025-05-22 passage and the 2025-05-22 passage but there is not one scene.
The divorce itself is missing: who filed, when, the court date, when it was final, the settlement, the day you left the house after keeping it a year, and where you went.

The June 6, 2014 DWI stop — the arrest that starts the jail chapter — is never told. Where were you coming from, what happened at the stop, and how did you end up in Hennepin County rather than Wright County?

Treatments are listed (Teen Challenge outpatient 2015, Hazelden 2016, Teen Challenge 2020) but not one has a scene. The reader needs at least one: what a first day looked like, and what leaving looked like.

Where does The Breaking end? the 2026-08-05 passage (August 2021 hospital vodka), the 2025-05-22 passage (dad: 'not worth saving'), and the 2026-08-29 passage (drinking to die, the vision) sit within weeks of each other in 2021. Say which of those is the last scene of this movement and which is the first scene of the next.

alternates.text:
Ash Wednesday: Tell Your Heart to Beat Again
The first song of Lent
I was trying to park a fifteen-passenger van in Chinatown when my life cracked open.
June 2014. I'd dropped the mission trip kids somewhere safe, and I was alone in that van, wedged between delivery trucks and tourists, when Danny Gokey's voice came through the speakers. And there was this line—about longing for the you that you used to be.
I couldn't move. Tears poured down my face in the middle of Manhattan, and I thought: I was doing great. I had a great marriage, a great family, a career I loved.
But that was a lie I was telling myself. Because by then, everything had already collapsed—I just hadn't admitted it yet.
***
The year before, my father had blown up my future. I had spent six months making every part of his business profitable—the rental cars, the trucking, the bus company, the storage. All of it. And I had a plan: buy him out, give him the retirement he said he wanted, take over the company I'd been running anyway.
The banker said yes. The CPA said yes. I needed nine Impalas—cars I could rent out and sell later for nearly what I paid. I had it mapped out to the dollar, to the month.
My dad came home from Florida, heard my plan, and got angry. He went to the Chevy dealer and bought thirteen Intrepids. Not nine. Not Impalas. Thirteen cars I had no reservations for, no use for, cars that would be worthless in six months. And he did it right before summer—when our two hundred fifty thousand dollars a month in school contracts disappeared.
That's when I gave up. Not dramatically. Quietly. I just stopped believing there was a way out. And I started drinking on purpose.
***
That same year, Joe and I went to San Francisco for our anniversary. He had plans I didn't know about—plans that involved getting me drunk and taking me to places where we'd have sex in public.
I didn't understand why he kept buying so much alcohol. I didn't understand until we were there, and I did what I always did. I never told him no.
The next morning, I stood at the window looking out over the city, thinking: How did my life get like this? This is not who I was made to be. I was a convicted Christian. I believed in honoring my marriage, honoring my parents. I thought I was doing everything right. But it had led me here—to this horrible, hollow place.
Joe got out of bed and came up behind me. He wrapped his arms around me, and it was the sweetest hug he'd given me since the day we were married. Long. Gentle. Tender.
And then he whispered: You are the best wife ever.
I felt rage rise up in me like nothing I had ever known. Because I had learned to be that wife. I had learned to cook, to host, to mother, to perform. I was a damn good wife. A damn good mother. And when he wanted it, I was a damn good whore too.
But standing at that window, being praised for my compliance the morning after being used—something in me finally saw the whole picture. And I hated him.
***
[SECTION TO CONTINUE: The therapist visit, the intentional love experiment, Joe's affair beginning October 2013, the DWI in June 2014, and circling back to the van in Chinatown and what this song means now, twelve years into recovery]
