passages.chat: ChatGPT · Victory letter draft
passages.text:
The Real Story

Frecka is based on a real person. Someone I loved. Someone who called me friend. Someone who—when the wind shifted and her rage finally found a target—decided to destroy me.

I still have a hard time believing all that happened to me.

I almost allowed my own destruction.

I’m grateful I have the evidence of her effort. Without it, I might have believed myself crazy. Without it, no one else would have believed me. Even with my evidence, some people still don’t believe. That’s fine. Prophets aren’t here to convince everyone.

This allegory isn’t revenge. It’s witness.

This is me saying: This happened. Here’s what it looked like from the inside. Here’s what envy does when it wears the mask of friendship. Here’s what it costs to be the target of someone else’s unspoken war.

And you know what else this is? It’s what it looks like to survive destructive, active, real hatred.

Why Allegory?

Sometimes the only way to tell the truth is to tell it slanted and sideways and upside down.

I couldn’t write a memoir. No matter how many years pass, I think it will remain too much. Too raw. Too real. Too emotional. Too explosive. 100% too much. Living it was too much. Healing from it was too much. Carrying it is too much.

But I can write about a creature on a camel, riding through a desert of her own making, watching her lies collapse one city at a time.

Allegory gave me distance. It gave me craft. It gave me the ability to see Frecka not as a villain to hate, but as a tragedy—a woman so hollowed out by jealousy and self-deception that she became a weapon against herself.

That’s not weakness on my part. That’s prophetic mercy. The kind that doesn’t excuse but refuses to dehumanize.

Why It Had to Come Out

The prophet Jeremiah said that when he tried to keep what he knew secret, the words felt like “fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9, ESV). He couldn’t not speak. It wasn’t about ego or platform or even courage. It was about survival.

That’s what this is for me.

Every time I tried to “let it go” or “move on” or “be the bigger person,” my stomach hurt. Not metaphorically. Physically. Like something was rotting inside me because I wasn’t letting the truth out.

So I spat it out. Onto the page. Into Frecka’s mouth. Into the desert, the mirrors, the valley of unheard prayers.

And my stomach stopped hurting.

What This Is (and Isn’t)

This is not a how-to guide for forgiveness.

This is not a tidy redemption arc.

This is not me saying that I’ve “released” anything into the light with a sage stick and an affirmation.

This isn’t fluff.

This is me saying: I saw what I saw. I’m not unsaying it. And I’m turning it into art because that’s the only way I know how to stay alive.

If you’ve ever been gaslit, slandered, or dismantled by someone who smiled while they did it—this is for you.

If you’ve ever had a stomachache that wouldn’t go away until you told the truth—this is for you.

If you’ve ever wondered whether you were the prophet or the villain in your own story—this is definitely for you.

A Note on Frecka

I gave her more dignity in fiction than she gave me in real life. I let her speak. I let her lie to herself. I let her walk through her own ruin with a kind of terrible, tragic grandeur.

Not because she deserves it. But because the truth is always more interesting than caricature.

And because if I’d written her as a flat villain, I’d have been lying too.

The Part I Almost Didn’t Say

There were visceral violations. Evidence left in my closet—things meant to humiliate. When I documented it, she called me delusional. For a while, I wondered if I was losing my mind. Turns out, I wasn’t crazy. And if it happened to you too—if someone planted evidence, rewrote your reality, made you question your own sanity while smiling in your face—you’re not crazy either.

If you’re carrying your own Frecka, your own desert, your own 252-page proof:

You saw what you saw.You survived what tried to destroy you.And you’re allowed to say it all out loud.

I hope you refuse to be silent. I hope you shout: You didn’t erase me! Thank you for the material. And I hope you shout it from the back of a fast camel who adores you

THE SHAMELESS SOPRANO


She sang the psalm like a siren.
No panties.
Also, no shame.
During the Liturgy.
While texting my husband.
I used to wonder how betrayal could hide in a hymn.
Now I know.
It harmonizes.
It smiles at your kids.
It blesses your food.
Then it takes your place.
But God hears the dissonance first.


 





THE ONE, THE WEASEL


Weasels slink.
Smile.
Sanctify themselves with charm.
She was my friend.
Until she was my replacement.
Until she weaponized empathy like a ninja in yoga pants.
Until her lies bought her glory.
Eventually weasels expose their teeth.
Today, I laugh.
A rodent is always a rodent.
I remade my henhouse.
And the rooster still roosters

Those ones are healing.

movements.name: The Rebuild
movements.note: This movement runs from the morning you woke up after trying to drink yourself to death (Oct 1, 2021) through 366 days at Teen Challenge, the sober house on Franklin and Chicago, the pee-collecting job, Mike's two cancelled weddings, and the woman your brother now calls calming. Its spine is surrender working itself out one next-right-choice at a time: the vision and the two verses, then ten months of rage, then the ACOA class that knocked you flat, then doors closing until you trusted yourself. What's strong: the jean jacket for April Lynn, the toothpaste aisle at Target, the choir van, Bill's 18 f-words, Vicky Dean asking what grounds you, and your brother's 'still so bossy.' What's thin: the actual arrival at Teen Challenge, Jakob's wedding from inside, the day you walked out, and the amends to Becca and Joe are all referred to but never told. The 55-word vignettes carry a lot of this movement's feeling but very few of them are anchored to a place, a date, or a named person; the questions below try to pin them down.
bigQuestions: The amends to Becca and Joe are nowhere in this file. When did you make them, in person or in writing, what did you say, and what did each of them say back? Was it a step in the program or something you did on your own?
Emily appears only as a birthdate (11.13.92) in the 13th Cluck. Who is Emily, and where does she enter the rebuild? Is 'meeting Emily' a scene the reader needs?

What was a plain day at Teen Challenge like from wake-up to lights out: the schedule, the 20-minute phone call, the uniform, the levels, the Saturdays out? The reader needs the rulebook once, early, so words like 'color' and 'level four' land later.
The arrival day and the graduation day (day 1 and day 366) are both missing. Two voice memos: walking in, walking out.
The granddaughters (Athena born early, 'tiny girls who each look like their daddies') are the rebuild's reward, but there is no scene of meeting them. What was the first time you held Athena?

alternates.note: Contains the identical 'In My Own Hand' epilogue paragraph about ten months of rage, word for word, wrapped inside the full thirteen-chapter Dry Bones allegory. The allegory is fiction written in Frecka's voice, not memoir, so the 2026-06-06 passage's shorter form wins for this movement.
alternates.text:
This is Dry Bones—my first subscriber-only piece. It’s thirteen chapters about envy, exile, and a camel who carries you even when she hates you. It’s allegorical, but it’s based on someone real. Someone who tried to erase me while smiling.

I’m sharing it here first, with you, because I need to know who’s in the room when I tell this story.

If you’re here—thank you. Now let’s walk into the desert.

Son of man, can these bones live?     - Ezekiel 37:3

Prologue · The Camel

The camel woke before I did and decided we were leaving. I let her think it was my idea. I am generous like that— though the way she looked at me suggested she knew better, and resented the charade.

The air tastes like copper and old perfume. Heat lays its hand on my neck. The saddle creaks a little confession every time I shift. I tell the beast her name is Vindication. She does not answer. Camels rarely flatter, and this one seems particularly disinclined to acknowledge me at all.

Behind me: a place that stopped saying my name. In front of me: a line the horizon draws because it enjoys watching me chase it. I don’t ask where we’re going. The camel knows. I’m here to look purposeful.

I brought essentials: a flask, a comb, a pocket mirror that lies kindly, and a few phrases that always worked on the weak—so concerned for her, only trying to help, you know how she is. Those are light to carry and heavy to throw.

A small wind lifts the edge of my scarf. It smells like something yellow, sun-sick, old. I tell myself it’s the desert. I tell myself many things. The camel keeps walking.

I am not fleeing. I am making an entrance somewhere else. That is the only story permitted.

The sun climbs. My shadow climbs with it, taller, thinner, less loyal. Sand grinds under the leather and makes a sound like teeth. If I close my eyes, I can hear applause. If I open them, only the silence claps.

We will arrive where I am already owed. That is how journeys work when you are me.

1 · Dust Behind Me

The wind repeats old headlines. Not the exact words—nothing so obvious. Just the tone. That little lift people do with their eyebrows when they’ve decided what you are.

Unstable. Dramatic. She performs pain.

I never needed them to believe all of it. Barely a mouthful will do. People finish their own poison.

The camel takes slow, righteous steps, as if counting my misdeeds for sport— or perhaps just counting the miles until she’s rid of me. I squeeze my knees and she refuses to hurry. Insolent creature. She moves like a priest: steady, unforgiven, bored with excuses, and deeply tired of hearing them.

Dust rises behind us in a soft, loyal cloud. I like that. I have always preferred followers who don’t ask questions. The human kind are so much worse—faces eager for stories, hands hungry for secrets. I fed them lines. They nodded. They always nod, until they don’t.

A memory blinks: two figures at a table, one too young to swallow what I served. He cried, briefly. I corrected the scene. No scandal, only rehearsal. No sin, only training. You know how she is. He believed me the way a drowning person believes in wood. Later, he learned to swim without me. Ungrateful, really.

The sun shifts. Sweat writes its own psalm down my spine. I adjust the reins and pretend the gesture means command. I have always been good at pretending command.

There is a rumor in the light today. It says: found out.

I smile. I have outlived rumors before. If you keep going, no one can place you where you were.

A name I used to wear tries to climb back on my tongue—one of the bright ones that bought me doors. I swallow. Names are heavy in heat. Better to travel as Frecka—short, sharp, unkind to say. It fits the air.

Something flickers at the edge of vision—antlers of heat, a crown of thorns made of sunlight, or perhaps nothing at all. I have seen worse. Once, in a room that smelled like leather and fear, the air pressed fingers to my throat. I spoke the Name that does not flatter me. The pressure vanished. I do not repeat that story. It makes the wrong person look strong.

The camel huffs—not at the fly, at me. Even insects know when to leave. She wishes I did.

Ahead, the horizon pretends to be new. Behind, the dust keeps my secrets until it doesn’t. That is the problem with witnesses—they love a breeze.

I catalogue assets: my posture, impeccable; my perfume, persuasive; my narrative, portable. I will arrive somewhere suitable and explain everything in a voice that sounds like mercy. They will be grateful I came. They will say I brought clarity. They will forget I brought matches.

The camel lowers her head and chooses a left I didn’t authorize. Fine. Let the servant feel clever. She’s carrying me, after all—the least I can do is pretend I’m steering. Though from the way her shoulders shift, I suspect she knows exactly how little I’m in control, and finds it grimly satisfying.

We pass a bleached branch that once tried to be a tree and failed. I salute it with two fingers. We can’t all be evergreen. Some of us must be iconic.

The wind shifts, brings me the faintest echo of a laugh. Not cruel. Worse—joyful. I know the owner of that sound. I dislike that it travels farther than mine.

Once, she asked me what I would do if he were mine—the one whose name I carried like proof of devotion. I thought about it longer than I should have, felt the truth surface before I could smooth it into something prettier. “I don’t think I want him,” I said. “I just want to win.” Her laugh was immediate, bright, certain I was performing wit instead of confessing strategy. I smiled and let her think so. The truth is lighter when people mistake it for a joke.

The camel keeps walking. I let her. I have time. And I have a story pocketed that can make even this heat look holy if I tell it right.

2 · The Desert of Names

The camel hums—a wet, patient gargle that sounds almost like prayer, or possibly complaint. Hard to tell the difference when you’re the subject of both. I tell her to hush; she continues. Obedience has never been one of my disciples, and she knows I have no real authority to command it.

Every few miles I drop a name into the sand to lighten the load. They used to glitter behind me like coins. Now they just sink.

The Girl with Three Rings—gone. The Siren of the Stage—gutted. The Prophet’s Friend—burned at the edges, still smoking somewhere behind us.

Each title had a season. Each season ended in applause that turned to rumor. The desert remembers everything but mercy.

Sometimes I catch the smell of my old names—sweet, spoiled fruit. They follow for a few yards, whispering the old adoration: you were dazzling, you were adored, you were almost divine. Almost. That word rubs like sand in a shoe.

I rename myself as we go, wishing for more each time. Frecka fits best: short, sharp, ugly enough to survive. It tastes like copper on my tongue, and the camel seems to approve.

A wind rises from nowhere and lifts my hair straight back. For a moment I see my reflection in the metal of my flask— eyes rimmed with red dust, crown of heat trembling above my head. Can that possibly be me? I look like a saint carved out of smoke.

The camel stumbles—or pretends to. The flask spills. Water meets sand and vanishes without thanks. When I look at her, one ear flicks. Not apology. Satisfaction.

I say, “We will find another name for me soon.” The camel grunts—not disagreement, exactly. More like the sound you make when forced to haul someone who keeps insisting the destination will be different this time, when you both know it won’t.

3 · Crossroads in the Sand

At noon the desert splits itself open. Four roads—thin, pale scars—cross one another like choices I’ve already made. The camel stops without my command; she knows indecision when she smells it. The air holds its breath. Even the flies circle wider, unwilling to choose a lane.

I shade my eyes and read the horizon. Every path glimmers as if promising water. Every promise tastes like metal.

The City of Mirrors. I know that one. Spent so many years there. Walls tiled in reflections, each face more devoted than the last. At first it was glorious—I could multiply forever. But reflections are hungry; they began to argue over which one of us was real. I left before they voted me out.

The Valley of Unheard Prayers. A fine quiet there. My kind of silence: thick, obedient, too polite to echo. I shouted blessings over the bones so I could hear my own authority. The wind coughed them back, sand filling every syllable. Silence that personal can bruise a person.

The Bazaar of Forgotten Names. I tried to sell my reputation there—a little tarnished but still recognizable. No buyers. They trade in newer scandals now, shinier shame. One merchant offered me a jug of anonymity for the whole bundle. I was tempted, but anonymity stains worse than infamy.

The House of the Silent Camel. The worst of them. Every beast stood motionless, eyes like blank coins, jaws locked. I walked among them whispering apologies, confessions, half-truths— nothing moved. It was like speaking to my own conscience: patient, unimpressed.

The camel under me snorts, breaking the spell. She angles her head west, where no road lies. A fifth direction—not mine, hers—drawn by hooves that have carried worse and survived to complain about it.

I pat her neck. “Fine. Take me where liars go when even hell is tired.” She grumbles as she kneels—not agreement, just resignation. She’ll take me there because that’s what camels do, not because I’ve earned the journey. When she rises again into the glare, her breath is sharp and impatient, as if daring me to thank her.

The crossroads fall behind, closing like a hand over its own scars. The desert swallows the sound of our going, and I pretend that means forgiveness.

4 · The City of Mirrors

The camel slows at a shimmer. From a distance it looks like water, but I recognize architecture disguised as mercy. The City of Mirrors always pretends to be salvation first.

I let her walk me in. Every wall blinks back my face—hundreds of me, each slightly improved. One taller, one thinner, one holy enough to quote scripture without smirking. They wave before I do. That’s the danger of devotion.

I whisper to the nearest reflection, “Remind them I was beloved.” She mouths the words perfectly but adds a tear. Show-off.

Further in, the streets narrow until mirrors face mirrors, multiplying me into a labyrinth of applause. I lose track of the real body. The camel refuses to follow; even she knows better than to compete with vanity.

I press my hand to a panel of glass. It ripples, cool as regret. Inside, another version of me mouths a warning— or maybe a curse. Hard to tell; I always look sincere when lying.

From somewhere above comes a cracking sound, a small fracture racing through ceilings of silver. Every copy freezes. For the first time, none of them look at me. They look behind me.

I turn. Nothing but the desert, wide and white. Still, the mirrors begin to turn cloudy, like breath on glass. They are forgetting me. Not as punishment—the mirrors aren’t moral, only honest. I’m just not interesting enough to hold their attention anymore. Even vanity has standards, and I’ve failed to meet them.

I back away. My reflection stays still. I leave before it decides to keep the life I borrowed.

Outside, the camel waits, chewing nothing, staring at the middle distance like she’s calculating how many more cities of my delusion she’ll be required to witness. I climb on. She doesn’t shift to help me settle—just stands there, stone-still, until I’ve hauled myself into place. The sand immediately begins to swallow my footprints. Even my shadow seems relieved to see me go, and the camel’s silence suggests she shares the sentiment.

We ride until the city shrinks to a glint, a single shard catching the sun— the last mirror that still remembers my name.

5 · The Valley of Unheard Prayers

The valley opens like a mouth that has forgotten how to bless. Air stands still here, heavy with salt and apology. Even the camel lowers her head, though not out of reverence. More like reluctance—the way you hesitate before entering a room where you know someone will ask you to do something thankless.

I tell her, “It’s only silence.” She snorts. Silence is the one thing animals never trust, especially when it’s wrapped around people who talk too much.

The sand changes color—paler, almost bone. I think it’s beautiful until I notice the shapes: knees, fingers, jawlines, all turned to limestone supplicants. A congregation of unfinished saints.

I climb down. The ground crunches. Someone’s rib becomes my stepping-stone. I try not to look reverent.

I lift my hands, remembering how I used to do it— palms high, voice pitched just right for pity. The first word dies halfway out. The valley eats it like bread.

I try again, louder, because louder always worked before. Still nothing. No echo, no wind, not even a polite hush of acknowledgment.

I used to pray for applause. Now I’d settle for feedback.

There’s a faint smell of smoke here, though nothing burns. It’s the scent of wishes evaporating. I inhale until it hurts.

The camel refuses to cross farther. She plants her feet, stubborn holiness in motionless form— or maybe just refusal to participate in another performance of piety that won’t change anything.

So I pray at her instead: “Carry me, O dumb creature, for I am weary of being divine.” Her eyelids drop, unimpressed. She’s heard it all before: the self-pity dressed as prayer, the complaint disguised as confession. And still she’ll carry me out, because that’s what she was made for— though her stillness makes it clear she doesn’t have to like it.

From the far ridge, thunder mutters like a forgotten god clearing his throat. I wait for rain. Only dust answers.

When I turn back, the valley has erased my footprints. Even my shadow lags, unwilling to follow.

I climb onto the camel again. She steps carefully—not out of reverence for the dead, but out of resentment for the living passenger who keeps dragging her through valleys where even prayers go to die.

I whisper, “We’ll find a place that still listens.” The camel’s ears flatten. The wind laughs—small, cruel, almost kind. She doesn’t.

6 · The Bazaar of Forgotten Names

The desert thins into noise. Color returns first—flags, tents, banners the color of bruised fruit. Then smell—dust mixed with cinnamon, rot mixed with perfume. The camel hesitates, as if we’ve stumbled into someone else’s memory. The Bazaar of Forgotten Names never dies; it just changes vendors.

I’ve been here before. Everyone has.

We pass rows of stalls where voices compete like crows. One woman sells absolution by the yard, folded in velvet and priced for the desperate. A man polishes halos for half a coin, no questions asked about provenance.

I recognize a merchant I once was. She wears my smile. Her table overflows with small metal tags, each stamped with a single word: Beloved. Redeemed. Important. Misunderstood. The cheaper ones read Influencer.

I reach for a tag stamped Vindicated—small, tarnished, but still legible. “How much?” I ask. The merchant looks at my hands, then at my face, calculating inventory. “What do you have?”

I pat my pockets: half a flask of sandwater, a cracked mirror, a story that used to make people weep. She shakes her head before I finish listing. “Those may still be valuable somewhere,” she says. “Just not here.”

I move to the next stall, then the next. Same answer everywhere. My currency—charm, narrative, the carefully curated version of myself—buys nothing in a market that trades in truth.

At the next booth a boy sells anonymity, bottled and pale. “Smells like mercy,” he says. I uncork it. It smells like nothing. That’s the point. But nothing is heavy once you try to carry it. I hand it back.

Farther down, a preacher calls bids for repentance—one sin per buyer, no refunds. He looks right at me and winks. I almost laugh. Even here, marketing survives.

Behind me, someone shouts my name—one of the old, beautiful ones. I almost turn. My body remembers the shape of that attention, the warmth of being recognized. But turning here costs more than I have left, and I already know: they’re not calling for me. They’re calling for the version I sold them years ago, the one who’s been dead longer than I’ve been willing to admit.

When I return to where I left her, the camel is chewing something invisible, her jaw working in slow, deliberate circles like she’s grinding her opinion of me into powder. She doesn’t look up when I approach. I climb on. She shifts her weight—not to balance me, but to remind me I’m a burden.

“Well,” I say, forcing brightness into my voice. “That was educational.” Her ears flick back. Not acknowledgment. Irritation. She starts walking before I’m fully settled, and I have to grab the saddle to keep from sliding off. It’s not an accident.

We leave the bazaar at dusk. The tents glow from within, a thousand fires spelling other people’s legends across the sand. I ride without speaking. The wind folds around us, whispering bargains I no longer believe. The desert accepts no receipts.

7 · The House of the Silent Camel

The road narrows to a hush. Even the wind walks barefoot here. Ahead, the dunes rise like walls, and between them rests a low building—mud-colored, roofless, ancient enough to have forgotten who built it.

The camel stops. She will go no closer.

I slide down, sand hissing at my horsey legs. “You could come with me,” I say. She turns her head away—deliberate, final. Not out of fear. Out of principle. She plants her feet, lowers her head, and exhales through her nostrils— the kind of breath that says, You want absolution? Walk in there yourself.

So I do.

Inside the doorway, shadow thickens. The air is warm, still, wrong. Dozens of camels stand shoulder to shoulder, silent as statues. Their eyes are blank coins. Their hides shimmer with sweat that never falls. The smell is sweet rot and patience.

I whisper, “I’ve come for counsel.” No movement. Only the faint rasp of my own breathing.

So I try honesty—carefully, like tasting poison: “I have lied,” I say. Nothing.

“I have loved badly.” Nothing.

“I have envied the light on another woman’s face.” Still nothing.

I kneel, dust catching in my throat. “I am tired,” I manage. That word ripples through the herd like a small wind. Several heads tilt toward me. Not mercy—recognition. Their gazes press until I feel the bones inside my skin shift, as if the truth is rearranging itself to fit.

I kneel there longer than I planned, waiting for the silence to crack. It doesn’t. The camels stand motionless, eyes fixed on something beyond me— or through me, as if I’m translucent, already halfway to erasure.

I try one more confession, this time without strategy: “I don’t know how to be anything other than this.”

The largest beast exhales—not a sigh, not judgment. Just breath. Old, patient, indifferent. The sound of a witness who has heard this story before and knows how it ends.

I back out slowly, my own breathing too loud in the stillness.

Outside, my camel waits exactly where I left her, chewing nothing, staring at the horizon like she’s calculating how many more miles of this performance she’ll have to endure.

When I climb into the saddle, she doesn’t acknowledge me. Just starts walking—not because I asked, but because standing still would mean staying in this place longer, and she’s as tired of it as I am.

We ride in silence for a long time. The sun climbs. The sand whispers. My throat is dry.

At last I say, “Well. That was useless.” The camel snorts—not agreement. Confirmation. She knew before we went in. She always knows. Dust blooms behind us like the last applause I’ll ever get, and even that sounds reluctant.

8 · The Siren of the Stage

We reach a plateau that looks like applause frozen mid-clap. The sand lies in ripples—each one a breath that never made it out. I tell the camel this is where I used to sing. She looks unimpressed; she always does— though this time there’s an extra weight to her indifference, as if she’s heard this nostalgic retelling before and knows it’s just another story I’m trying to believe about myself.

There was once a man with a voice big enough to hide inside. He sang and the crowd leaned toward him the way flowers chase sun. I mistook that warmth for worship and stepped into it.

I didn’t love his music. I loved that people listened when he sang—leaned forward, held their breath, forgot themselves for the length of a chorus. I thought if I stood close enough, some of his joy would spill onto me. It did, briefly—but only long enough for them to wonder why I was still there after the song ended.

I remember the stage lights: too white, too close, the kind of brightness that scrubs you clean of truth. I remember his back— the way it held every note and never once turned fully toward me.

I matched his pitch because I wanted what he had to offer. Devotion. I smiled because envy looks better when you drape it in harmony and call it collaboration. When people clapped, I bowed deeper than he did; they thought it was humility. It was hunger.

Afterward he asked why I never sang my own song. I told him, “Because yours has better acoustics.” He laughed. Everyone laughs before they understand.

The camel’s hooves drum a steady rhythm beneath me— thud, thud, pause—like a metronome for regret, or possibly a countdown to the moment she’s finally allowed to stop.

The air here still vibrates faintly, as if the last note refuses to die. I hum to test the echo. It does not return.

“You hear that?” I ask her. She flicks an ear—not curiosity. Irritation. As if to say, Of course nothing comes back. Why would it? “Nothing comes back anymore,” I say. Her silence is its own answer: It never did. You just weren’t listening.

I straighten in the saddle, pretend I’ve finished a performance. The audience, mercifully, is gone. Only the desert remains—wide, impartial, immune to charm.

We move on. Behind us the wind rearranges the dunes into rows of empty seats. For a moment, it almost sounds like clapping.

9 · The Girl with Three Rings

We travel through a plain so flat it feels judged. The sun makes a sound like bees against the skull. Even the camel seems subdued, her footsteps small and deliberate.

This is the place for that story—the one about the three. I try to keep it brief, but memory is a performer that refuses to leave the stage.

There were three of them once, each promising forever in a slightly different key. I accepted all offers. Why choose a song when you can conduct the choir?

I wore the rings stacked—tiny crowns for each finger. I wore three because one felt like settling, like choosing a single melody when you could conduct the whole choir. Why choose when you can collect? I thought I was building a kingdom. Turns out, you can’t rule men who don’t know they’re subjects—and who leave the moment they discover the crown was always costume jewelry.

The weight made my hands ache, but beauty always charges a tax. When I waved, they glittered; when I prayed, they clinked; when I lied, they caught the candlelight and applauded.

My mother found out—sweet woman, devoted, the kind who believes honesty is a sacrament you can’t skip just because it’s inconvenient. She gave me an ultimatum dressed as mercy: “You tell them, or I will.” So I did. Not because conscience moved me, but because exposure was coming either way, and I preferred to control the narrative.

The jovial one ended it the moment I confessed. Clean break. No negotiation. No second chance. He married someone else years later. For a long time, we were neighbors, close enough I could see him through the kitchen window: a man who kept his vow to be done with me, building a life so close I can watch it bloom while mine… doesn’t.

The honest one looked at me as if I were a riddle he’d solved too late. He said, “You’re disgusting. Begone.” I wasn’t offended. I was impressed—finally, someone who wouldn’t let me sand down the edges or reframe the scene or spin his disgust into misunderstanding. He saw me clearly and walked away without apology. Even I can respect a vow kept that clean. I long for him still.

Only the boring one stayed. Married me, even. He wasn’t bothered by the others; he was excited by them. All those men wanting me—that was the prize, not me. Proof I was worth collecting, even if I wasn’t worth keeping. So I married him. Not because I loved him. Because he loved that other men did.

On the drive home from confessing, she sat beside me in the car— the one who always prayed for people, even when they didn’t deserve it. She said, “My prayer for you is that one day you can just be yourself, who you were created to be.”

I thanked her. I meant it, briefly.

But prayers like that require honesty, and honesty requires a witness I can’t rewrite or charm or redirect. So I chose men who didn’t ask too many questions, men who believed my performances were the same as my person. And when that stopped working, I chose another.

The camel trudges on, each step heavy with something that feels like contempt. She doesn’t care about my heartbreaks. She just knows she’s been conscripted to carry them.

I tell her, “He could have adored me if he’d understood me.” She shakes her head—not disagreement, exactly. More like the gesture you make when someone insists the problem was everyone else’s comprehension, and you’re too tired to correct them.

I hold up my hand to the sun. The indentations where the rings once sat are still visible— thin white ghosts circling my fingers, tiny halos that refused to stay gold.

Somewhere in the heat, I think I hear metal hit stone— a final ring dropped, rolling toward forgetfulness. The sound fades fast.

“Good,” I tell the camel. “I shook off the dust.”

She makes no reply. Her next step isn’t lighter—it’s resigned. She’ll carry me because that’s what camels do, not because I’ve earned the journey or learned anything worth carrying forward.

10 · Why They Choose Her

We pass into cooler air. Evening again. The sky burns down to a rim of brass and everything smells like endings. The camel slows; she knows this stretch. It’s the road where envy learned my name.

I used to stand beside her—the one the crowds noticed first. Same sun, same breeze, same dust on our skirts. Still, people drifted toward her as if she carried light in her pockets. They spoke to me only when she looked away.

I didn’t want to be her. I wanted to beat her—to prove that devotion could be learned, that warmth was just a performance I hadn’t mastered yet. But you can’t beat someone who isn’t keeping score. That was the part that made me furious: she loved people the way rain falls, without permission or calculation, and they loved her back just as freely. None of it was strategic. She wasn’t even trying to win, which made every one of my losses unbearable.

I practiced her laugh until my throat ached. I borrowed her kindness in small doses, wore it like perfume and wondered why it never stayed. Kindness, it turns out, isn’t transferable—you can’t borrow it like a scarf and expect it to fit the same. Envy, though? That travels just fine. Packs light. Follows you everywhere.

I learned to narrate my own diminishment— “Oh, she’s the gracious one. I’m the younger one.” It worked for a while. Clever can dazzle, but never comfort.

The camel trudges. Her tail swats the air like punctuation— sharp, dismissive, the way you swat at something persistent and annoying.

I say, “You’ve seen her. You know she isn’t that radiant.” The camel does not answer, and somehow that’s worse. Her silence isn’t neutral. It’s the silence of someone who’s heard you lie so many times they’ve stopped correcting you, because what’s the point?

Once I asked the question aloud, to her: why do they choose you? The silence that followed was the kind that smiles. She didn’t know either. I don’t think she even thought about it.

If jealousy has a shape, it is the circle I walked that day— round and round until I dug my own altar. The offering was joy; the idol was comparison.

The first miracle I ever witnessed was people loving her without agenda or applause. The second was me surviving it, walking away with my spine still ramrod straight. The third—still waiting on that one—would be learning to want something other than first place in a race no one else was running.

11 · The Throne of Sand

The next dawn arrives sharp and colorless, the sort that doesn’t bother with mercy. I tell the camel we’re stopping. She lowers her head—not prayer, exhaustion. Or possibly relief that I’ll be off her back for a few hours. I take it as consent, though her stillness feels more like tolerance.

There’s a rise ahead—a dune just high enough for ceremony. I climb it, knees sinking, the sand hissing under every step. At the top I drop my pack and start to build.

It begins as play: handfuls of dust shaped into steps, a seat, a suggestion of grandeur. Soon I’m sweating, working in rhythm, muttering blueprints. The wind lends applause. I pretend not to notice it laughing.

When the shape is finished, it almost resembles a throne— crooked, shimmering, absurd. I brush my palms together, declare myself returned to sovereignty. From this height I can almost see redemption. I can almost believe it’s waving.

But sand is a petty material. It shifts when praised. By midday the left arm of the throne slides away; by evening the seat itself collapses, dumping me unceremoniously back to my knees.

I curse the architecture. The camel grunts—not approval, exactly. More like the sound you make when someone finally admits what you’ve known all along: nothing they build will stand.

I rebuild smaller, meaner. No throne now—just a mound, a platform for denial. I plant my mirror in it like a flag and practice my expression of triumph. The reflection trembles, warped by heat.

“You never were made for ruling,” I tell her. The reflection answers with my own mouth: “You never were made for truth.”

The wind shifts, and my kingdom joins the others buried out here— cities of mirrors, valleys of prayers, forgotten bazaars. All of it dust again.

I sit in the wreckage until night takes the color out of everything. The camel kneels beside me—not out of affection, but duty. Uninvited, unappreciated, and deeply aware of both. When she exhales, her breath carries grit and something like grace, though the grace feels accidental, a by-product of simply existing near someone this broken.

“I’m still queen of something,” I whisper. She blinks once, long and slow— the way you blink at someone who’s still clinging to a title no one else remembers granting them.

I won, finally. Took the man I didn’t want from the woman I couldn’t beat, claimed a prize that felt hollow the moment I held it. Victory tastes like copper and disappointment—turns out, winning isn’t the same as arriving, and arrival without destination is just another kind of exile.

Then, finally, she stands—not because I’ve finished my confession, but because she’s finished listening. It’s time to go, and her rising feels less like compassion and more like the end of a shift she didn’t volunteer for.

12 · Revelation

Night folds over us like a shawl gone thin with use. The camel’s hooves make no sound now; it’s as if she’s learned stealth from guilt— or maybe just exhaustion, the kind that comes from hauling someone who keeps insisting the next mile will be different.

The stars blink in patterns I used to call divine. Tonight they look like eyes.

Something rides with me. Not beside—within. A whisper that breathes when I do, a queenly echo that corrects my posture when I slouch. She hums under my ribs, old as deceit. When I speak, she chooses the words. When I fall silent, she finishes the sentence anyway.

I ask her name and feel her smile. “You’ve worn it often,” she says.

I understand then: she isn’t new. She’s been with me since I learned how to win instead of love, since I discovered that devotion could be performed and performance could pass for devotion if you smiled right.

I remember her voice in the City of Mirrors, how it coached the reflections to applaud. I remember her perfume in the Valley of Unheard Prayers, how it smothered the silence until even God lost interest. She was in the Bazaar, haggling for my identity. She was in the House of the Silent Camel, the one voice I couldn’t imitate because it was the only one that was mine.

Now she whispers, “You are still mine.” I almost agree. Habit, mostly.

The camel stops. Not gradually—just stops, mid-step, as if she’s hit an invisible wall. I lurch forward, grab the saddle to keep from falling.

“What—?”

She turns her head. Slowly. Deliberately. Her eye catches starlight and throws it back at me— not a warning, exactly. More like a mirror held up by someone who’s tired of watching me lie to myself and has decided, just this once, to let me see what she sees.

In that eye I see: Every manipulated conversation. Every borrowed kindness I wore like costume jewelry. Every man I collected to prove I was worth collecting. Every time I chose winning over being known.

And underneath all of it—the voice. The queenly echo. The thing I’ve been calling strategy, calling survival, calling me.

The camel doesn’t blink. Doesn’t look away. Just stands there, holding the mirror steady, daring me to keep pretending I don’t see it.

“No,” I say aloud, testing the sound.

The desert listens. The voice inside me hisses—pleasure, maybe, or pain. It fades a little, like smoke dissipating when you open a window.

I breathe deep until my lungs ache, tasting sand and copper and something else— something that might be air without perfume, words without spin, silence without performance.

For the first time in years, the air smells only of sand.

“I can walk from here,” I tell the camel.

She doesn’t stop me. Just kneels—not gently, not cruelly. Just kneels, the way you kneel when you’ve carried something too long and too far, and someone finally says they’ll take it from here.

I slide down and stand barefoot in the cooling dust.

Somewhere behind my ribs, a door creaks shut. Somewhere beyond the horizon, a woman-shaped shadow begins to scream— the queenly echo realizing she’s been named, confronted, abandoned.

I let her. I keep walking.

The camel watches me go, then turns and walks the other direction— not toward anything, just away. Her duty is finished. I don’t call her back.

I called her Vindication in the beginning—tried to name her the way you name a thing you think you own. She never answered. Not once in all these miles.

I thought it was because camels don’t flatter royalty. Now I understand: she wasn’t mine to name. She was never part of my story. She was just a camel, conscripted into carrying me, who finally got to walk away.

For the first time since we started this journey, I understand: I chose this. All of it. And now I choose to walk away.

13 · The End of the Road

The sand finally stops pretending to be a road. It flattens into a colorless plain—no mirage, no shimmer, just horizon stretched too thin to hold another lie.

I think of how it ended with Vindication. She just halted. Her breath sounded like the last note of a hymn no one remembers— or possibly the sound of relief, finally permitted. She knelt without command; we both knew the ride was finished. She had carried me as far as duty required, and not one step farther.

I remained in the seat for a while, waiting for the usual script to begin: someone rushing out with forgiveness, a sudden wind arranging itself into applause, a miracle timed to my convenience.

None of that happens. The wind is a blank page. The sky refuses to sign its name.

When I finally slid off, the sand gave a sigh— relief, not grief.

This walk is miserable. My feet sink. The ground feels warm, alive, disgusted. Every step forward drags the smell of old perfume out of me. It’s faint now, a ghost of flattery and fear.

I taste metal again—copper, maybe guilt. The taste you get when you’ve bitten your own tongue too long.

The camel sees me from a distance. Her eyes aren’t patient—they’re tired. Ancient, yes. Unoffended, no. If she could speak, she would say what every conscripted witness eventually says: I warned you. I carried you anyway. Now I’m done.

The camel turns away first—not out of mercy, but relief. She’s carried me as far as duty requires. Now she walks toward nothing, unburdened, and I understand: that emptiness is a reward for her, not a punishment.

The horizon wobbles; I realize it isn’t distance—it’s reflection. The desert has turned into a mirror after all, only this one doesn’t flatter. It shows a woman made of dust and echo, a face soft around the edges from too many borrowed identities.

I reach out. The image ripples. No one reaches back.

For a moment, pity flares— not theirs for me, mine for her, the image of one who believed that winning was the same as being chosen.

Then the wind blows again, and the mirror breaks, and she scatters— a thousand tiny Freckas swirling upward, turning into nothing the color of forgiveness.

I look down and see the camel’s faint trail. Her tracks lead nowhere, which is, at last, an honest destination— and one she’s earned by hauling me across a desert I insisted on crossing.

I follow on foot, lighter than I have any right to be.

EPILOGUE · In My Own Hand

I wrote Frecka because I needed her out of my blood. She had been living there rent-free—eating the oxygen, drinking from my joy like it was a cup she deserved. She’s quiet now. Not gone, just smaller. A dust mote in the corner of memory. And you know the thing about dust motes? They don’t matter.

Sometimes I still feel her stir when I’m tired or brilliant or both, and I whisper, stay down, darling, we’re doing something different now.

There’s a kind of holiness in seeing your villain as a flawed human. It keeps the story from turning you into her.

Think about it like this: Pity is not permission, it’s proof that you survived with your heart intact.

For me, writing is the exorcism. Ink and truth and humor do the work that rage cannot. I don’t know how to live with rage. I tried. For ten solid months. November 2021 all the way through May 2022. Rage takes… everything. The day I let it go, I started living again. Wholly, unabashedly, unashamed.

So if she ever reads this— and she will, because people like her always check to see who’s still watching— I hope she recognizes herself long enough to flinch. Then I hope she sets it down and walks outside and smells the wind and wonders, for one trembling second, if there’s still a way back.

And there certainly is a way back.

Redemption is not mine to give or withhold. It’s already flaming freely, an offer from our Father who drops literally everything and runs joyfully to welcome us the second we turn homeward.

Even stinking of pig poo and poor choices.

Even with sand in our teeth and envy in our pockets.

Even after a decade in the desert, naming camels we don’t own and building thrones that won’t stand.

Isn’t that magnificent? The Father is already running. All any of us has to do is turn around.

I can’t stay and watch to see if she turns to our Father. I can only join the celebration once she does.

Isn’t that also magnificent? That there’s enough for all of us?

Author’s Note: On Prophets, Stomachaches, and Telling the Truth

I didn’t sit down to write Dry Bones for altruistic reasons. I wrote it because if I didn’t, it was going to eat me alive from the inside out.

Someone once called me a prophet. More than one someone, really. I shrug it off and ignore that title, that definition—partly because I didn’t think I deserved a title, and mostly because I don’t always understand what it means. I thought prophets were people who predicted the future or performed miracles or at least had their lives together. I thought prophets were all dead men who went a little crazy. I thought it meant you had to live in a desert and die of starvation.

Turns out, that’s not it at all.

A prophet is someone who sees what’s true when everyone else is committed to the lie—and then says it out loud, even when it costs them everything. Prophets don’t get halos. They get stomachaches. They get accused of being bitter, dramatic, unforgiving. They get told to “move on” by people who never had to carry what they’re carrying.

But they do it anyway. Because the alternative—swallowing it, pretending it didn’t happen, letting the lie win—is worse than any accusation. The alternative is death.

The Real Story

Frecka is based on a real person. Someone I loved. Someone who called me friend. Someone who—when the wind shifted and her rage finally found a target—decided to destroy me.

I still have a hard time believing all that happened to me.

I almost allowed my own destruction.

I’m grateful I have the evidence of her effort. Without it, I might have believed myself crazy. Without it, no one else would have believed me. Even with my evidence, some people still don’t believe. That’s fine. Prophets aren’t here to convince everyone.

This allegory isn’t revenge. It’s witness.

This is me saying: This happened. Here’s what it looked like from the inside. Here’s what envy does when it wears the mask of friendship. Here’s what it costs to be the target of someone else’s unspoken war.

And you know what else this is? It’s what it looks like to survive destructive, active, real hatred.

Why Allegory?

Sometimes the only way to tell the truth is to tell it slanted and sideways and upside down.

I couldn’t write a memoir. No matter how many years pass, I think it will remain too much. Too raw. Too real. Too emotional. Too explosive. 100% too much. Living it was too much. Healing from it was too much. Carrying it is too much.

But I can write about a creature on a camel, riding through a desert of her own making, watching her lies collapse one city at a time.

Allegory gave me distance. It gave me craft. It gave me the ability to see Frecka not as a villain to hate, but as a tragedy—a woman so hollowed out by jealousy and self-deception that she became a weapon against herself.

That’s not weakness on my part. That’s prophetic mercy. The kind that doesn’t excuse but refuses to dehumanize.

Why It Had to Come Out

The prophet Jeremiah said that when he tried to keep what he knew secret, the words felt like “fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9, ESV). He couldn’t not speak. It wasn’t about ego or platform or even courage. It was about survival.

That’s what this is for me.

Every time I tried to “let it go” or “move on” or “be the bigger person,” my stomach hurt. Not metaphorically. Physically. Like something was rotting inside me because I wasn’t letting the truth out.

So I spat it out. Onto the page. Into Frecka’s mouth. Into the desert, the mirrors, the valley of unheard prayers.

And my stomach stopped hurting.

What This Is (and Isn’t)

This is not a how-to guide for forgiveness.

This is not a tidy redemption arc.

This is not me saying that I’ve “released” anything into the light with a sage stick and an affirmation.

This isn’t fluff.

This is me saying: I saw what I saw. I’m not unsaying it. And I’m turning it into art because that’s the only way I know how to stay alive.

If you’ve ever been gaslit, slandered, or dismantled by someone who smiled while they did it—this is for you.

If you’ve ever had a stomachache that wouldn’t go away until you told the truth—this is for you.

If you’ve ever wondered whether you were the prophet or the villain in your own story—this is definitely for you.

A Note on Frecka

I gave her more dignity in fiction than she gave me in real life. I let her speak. I let her lie to herself. I let her walk through her own ruin with a kind of terrible, tragic grandeur.

Not because she deserves it. But because the truth is always more interesting than caricature.

And because if I’d written her as a flat villain, I’d have been lying too.

The Part I Almost Didn’t Say

There were visceral violations. Evidence left in my closet—things meant to humiliate. When I documented it, she called me delusional. For a while, I wondered if I was losing my mind. Turns out, I wasn’t crazy. And if it happened to you too—if someone planted evidence, rewrote your reality, made you question your own sanity while smiling in your face—you’re not crazy either.

If you’re carrying your own Frecka, your own desert, your own 252-page proof:

You saw what you saw.You survived what tried to destroy you.And you’re allowed to say it all out loud.

I hope you refuse to be silent. I hope you shout: You didn’t erase me! Thank you for the material. And I hope you shout it from the back of a fast camel who adores you.

Now go be brilliant.

— Kari

chapters.why: Mid-program, once you were trusted with the birthdays; the first time the movement shows grace going out from you instead of into you.
questions: 'maybe it was just a moment that went sideways' between you and April Lynn. What was the moment?

What were the 'quite charming and lovely' things you learned about April Lynn and shared at her birthday? Name one or two.

passages.chat: ChatGPT · Cackle-tale Trauma Podcast
passages.text:
That's Tiffany. However, it's not my story. Let's talk about April Lynn. So, April Lynn and I were at Teen Challenge together, and we didn't get along. Which was mostly my fault, surprisingly. I normally get along with everybody, but I just... There was something that rubbed me wrong about her. Or maybe it was just a moment that went sideways, or whatever, but... We just... I didn't like her. And she avoided me, probably because I didn't like her. So, I was in charge of the birthdays at Teen Challenge. And so I would spend time with each lady as their birthday approached, and visit with them. Learning things that I could share with the group on the day of their birthday. And I would collect things from others to give as a gift. Because nobody had money, but we could share things. And so, we got all done, got all ready for her birthday, and I packed it up and brought it down there. And I put my jean jacket in there, because I didn't like it. It was stiff, blah, blah, blah. And so I just thought, I'm going to give it to her. Because she kept saying to me, like, I really like your jacket, blah, blah, blah. And it was really the best thing I had to give her. So, I put it in there. We get down there, and I get up and I introduce her. And I'm like, let me tell you about this lady. And shared the stories that I learned about her, which were quite charming and lovely. And then she came up, and we sang to her, and we prayed over her, and then she got her gift. And when she pulled that jacket out, she started crying. Which, honestly, she was a crier, so it wasn't that unusual. But it was so beautiful in that moment that my heart just expanded. And I saw in that moment what grace was. Like, we get stuff, and then we give it away. And somehow that does something for the other, for the receiver. And, I mean, it's a lot more than a jean jacket. So, let's use that story.

passages.chat: Claude · Structuring a two-part memoir around the number thirteen
passages.text: I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. That's what the whole question was about. I mean, this this this is a really different book to write than it would have been even two years ago, and certainly certainly a different book than it would have been four years ago. And by far, a different book than it would be if I wrote it in two years, but I'm losing the sense of what that was like to be a teacher on this for a year and battling these things that were built up over a lifetime that were not my fault. The trauma that I lived to was real, and it created a lot of effects in me to the point where, like, that when I started doing ACOA at the adult children of health class at Teen Challenge, it was late in my program. I had already, I think, surrendered to the notion of real recovery means I'm gonna go through some hard stuff. And I thought I was doing that, but then I went in that class, and I realized that everything I am was shaped by a woman who hated me, my mother, because of her own wounding. And and so as much as I thought I was this unique person, you know, uniquely and wonderfully created by my creator, I I I knew that from the start. But what it looked like when I went in that class was... I was cliche because of who my mother was, and it was dismayed to me. Like, so dismaying that I actually had, like, a... I don't know what you call it. Like, if it was a real live anxiety attack to the point where I I was at a choir event, and I was being forced to go up there and singing the choir for two challenge. And I I couldn't stop. Like, tears were just leaking out of me. Like, I couldn't even... and it had been a horrific ride there. Like, they drove these fifteen passenger vans. Like, they were fucking race car drivers. And, I mean, it was it was such a bad day, and I I told the girl, I'm like, my my trauma and my wounding and my feeling is not entertainment for these people. Don't make me go up there. And she said, well, if you don't go up there, you're gonna be out of color, which would have been disciplinary action, which would have meant I couldn't have any of the perks that at that point were really, like, I... because I got to get out for eight hours on Saturdays because of where I was in my program, and I needed those eight hours to keep my sanity at that point. That place was driving me crazy. And so I I surrendered to that having to perform in the middle of what was very traumatizing. And so I I don't want the realness of that to go away. I don't wanna diminish what happened to me. But I do wanna say that there's something on the other side of it.

passages.chat: ChatGPT · Comment war analysis
passages.text:
Omgosh!!! I don’t have a single bad thing to say about staff!  Nor am I saying a bad thing about teen challenge. I am, however, reporting facts. 

I was deeply traumatized by things that happened at MNTC. And when I graduated, I was forced to go to unsafe and unhealthy places. 

During that time, though we know the value of peer support in early recovery, I was not contacted once for supportive reasons which made me feel as though I was worth more to MNTC as a relapse than a success. 

And yet, I am contacted regularly - at a cost of thousands of dollars I might add - for donations. 

MnTC forces people on stages, slaps a “falling down drunk” label on them, and then rattles the collection plate — all while sitting on $135 million. That isn’t about paying light bills or keeping beds full. Profit off pain dressed up as piety.

And don’t tell me I don’t understand billing. I’ve been behind the curtain. I know what those ledgers look like. I’ve worked on the billing/business side of recovery as well. My stay was not paid by donations; I have the receipts. Yet congregations were spoon-fed the story that their checks kept me alive. That’s not ministry. That’s manipulation with a choir in the background.

So yes — I honor the staff on the ground. But the machine behind them? The one that trades people’s rawest wounds for donor dollars? That’s the part that’s gross. And I’ll keep saying it, because my life depended on the truth — not the marketing.

passages.chat: Claude · Finding light in darkness during loss
passages.text:
So when i got in trouble over my mom’s stuff. The detectives called my sister in for the investigation. And she THREW me under the bus and then drove the bus over me multiple times. She wanted to protect herself and did. We were co everything. Guardians and conservators and I’m the only one who got in trouble. She’d married a rich guy so she hired lawyers. I couldn’t. I was in the midst of poverty and about to get worse. I was drinking and unable to stand on my own. I asked her and dad for help legally and neither would. So i couldn’t defend myself against the law firm and new conservator. And then it became criminal because the assertetion  was that I had used 107k of moms money myself. 

My records proved I didn’t so the 7 felony charges were reduced to one charge of failure to fiduciary stuff. All it took was my lawyer actually looking at my records to see if recoded everything and they dropped six of the charges. Immediately. After something like four years of shit. It was the month after I was out of mntc so I was so relieved that I just pled guilty. I should not have. I should have gone to trial. 

So my sisters convincing lies and now belief that I stole money stands. And she won’t talk about it.

questions: How long were you at the sober house on Franklin and Chicago, and how did you get there from Teen Challenge? Was it your choice or were you 'forced to go to unsafe and unhealthy places' as the 2025-08-21 passage says?
What happened on the bus ride that made it 'very stressful' and 'very scary'? Give one concrete thing you saw or that happened to you on it.
Who is 'she' in the 2025-05-09 passage's Probation hair check: a probation officer, sober house staff, or Teen Challenge? Where did the check happen?
Who was your first real friend at the sober house, and how did that start?

passages.chat: ChatGPT · Cackle-tale Trauma Podcast
passages.text: Here's an example of how hard it was to find true healing. After I graduated from the Team Challenge 12-month program, and was there for 366 days, I was living in a sober house in Minneapolis, on the corner of Franklin and Chicago, a very scary place in the city. And I had to ride the bus over to Target to get a couple things. One of the things I needed was toothpaste, and I don't remember the rest. But I do remember getting to Target after a very stressful bus ride from a very dangerous place, and going to the aisle where the toothpaste was, and just being overwhelmed by the amount of toothpaste, by the fact that everything was locked and you had to call for help, and just not knowing what to do. I ended up leaving and crying all the way home on the very scary bus, so I had to go back and get toothpaste later. It was very hard to heal.

passages.chat: Claude · Brain is mustard book revision
passages.text:
Oh. yeah. I don't spend money or dream about it until it's in my pocket. Weird writing and ideas aside, I'm remarkably low key. 

Also, this is more than just work. There's something about calling. I've had money all my life. It's not the money that matters - or at least it didn't matter until I didn't have it. I have pulled myself up, started working again after the 12 months i was forced to sit still in recovery programming, and took a job collecting urine for drug testing. from there I took every reasonable job i was offered including peer support (i'm fully certified) untiil I was able to live comfortably. I have been able to get off of all public support including health insurance.

I'm capable of remarkable things, Monet. I'm glad your'e the voice of reason. But we're going to build something pretty kick ass.



---

passages.chat: Claude · Daily writing prompt for Christmas Eve
passages.text: What it looked like in my life was all these doors that kept closing to me during recovery. Like, in most of my life, I was a very I don't know, central figure, popular with people. I had a lot of friends. I had a of activities. Everybody said yes to me. Everybody. I was very dynamic, and charismatic. And then I got in recovery, and I was like, the pariah. Like, nobody I I didn't really make friends easily. Nothing happened easily for me. The things I wanted to do in recovery, like, the job I wanted was the sound system, and I ended up having to clean the kitchen. Like, seriously. And and even, like, musically, like, I've always been center stage with the piano and whatever, and I and I just I couldn't find that recovery. And then even the jobs after recovery were, like, collecting pee from for urine samples and doing the dumbest stuff ever, but it led me to this glorious place I'm at today where I trust myself again. And it was almost like every time I circled through another no and rejection, I found another healing and another way to get closer to what I was supposed to be doing.

passages.chat: Scripture and music in worship
passages.text: Well, did I ever tell you that I was gonna marry Mike, and I was gonna marry him twice, actually. So I have had a very interesting, like, romantic history. And so along the way, I met Mike on plenty of Tinder, I think, and we started out by talking on the phone, and eventually it became, like, because of COVID, it became more on the phone. But then eventually, we met in real life. And, honestly, if I met him in real life first, I never would have dated him. because he's not very physically attractive to me. And, also, there are things about him in person, like, that I didn't know about until I met him. And so so, anyway, so I... the relationship progressed, and eventually, he was the one person who came to visit me every single time I could have visitors at Team Challenge, which meant said... which meant that he came one night a week for two hours. And then on Saturdays, he came for three hours. And then when it got to the point where I could have hours out of Team Challenge, he was reliable and showing up and taking me out of Teen Challenge to go do stuff. And those visits were very, very important to me because I was otherwise very cloistered. I got twenty minutes of a phone call a day for a year. and I I mean, I did workarounds to that, which we'll talk about in a minute. But I also, really depended on him. He was so kind to me, and he made sure I had things that I needed and many things I wanted. And he made that ear bearable for me. And so after I got out, we were gonna get married on one twelve thirty one whatever that year was. So it would have been one two three one two three. So twenty twenty three, that would have been. Twelve thirty one twenty three. Anyway, he... the week before the wedding was supposed to happen, he... in our therapy session with Marty said that he wasn't gonna come. And so that was the end of that. Well, we became friends again, and eventually we decided to try again. So we were gonna give married on September thirteenth twenty twenty four, I believe. And, so everybody, Jakob and Nicole got a plane ticket. They were coming back. brother-in-law, and it turned out that he was such a douche about the baby. So Athena was born early. And so the Sunday before our wedding was supposed to be, he was being a big douche about it, and I wanted to go see her, and he wasn't getting ready and stuff like that. And I said, oh my god. I do not much spend my life with this man. And about a month prior to that, pastor David had told me to postpone the wedding because he just didn't think it was a right thing, blah blah blah. But I just thought he was wrong. And so on that Tuesday before the wedding again, I said to him finally, I'm like, Mike, are you coming to our wedding? And he said, No. And I said, you are the biggest fuck I've ever met, and I left. I asked I asked permission, actually, of my therapist. I said, can I go? And she said, Kari, you can go. And so the second time, that was the end of it. Like, but now we're friends. It's all fine. I don't have a grudge against him. I actually think it was God protecting me from a really, really big mistake. And so I'm really glad for the way things turned out, but it it kinda speaks to that thing because Mike... that's too much for Mike. He couldn't handle my joy, and he couldn't handle my I I feel like what he couldn't handle was this child like delight, I guess. He calls it a child like delight that I have on wonder in the world. Like, when I drive around the corner and I see the Stone Arch Bridge, pretty much every day, I'm like, oh my gosh. That's so beautiful. Or I see flowers, like, blooming, and I'll be like, oh my gosh. You finally bloom. And he's like, you said that yesterday. And he just he just couldn't understand that awe and wonder I have in the world, and it was too much for him. And I I think that's why we're not married. I think that's why he couldn't bear to go through with it or whatever. But, honestly, it doesn't feel like a rejection because I already knew it wasn't the right thing. know if that makes any sense at all. So she had to be the one that would say he wouldn't come, I think, because I'm not a rejecter of people. I have... they have to be the ones that do the ending of this situation or whatever, which, by the way, I'm working on. But... okay. So that whole story just to explain that... to explain that I'm aware that I'm too much at... for people.

chapters.title: A sisterhood of snorters
chapters.why: Laughter coming back: the snort in group, the fake laugh with Amber that turned real, the therapist who lost it. The vignettes that belong to the rebuild.

passages.text:
She snorted in group once.
Ugly laugh. Real laugh.
It cracked my grief open.
I was still detoxing from all the pretending.
And she seemed so unfiltered.
Unapologetic even.
She made recovery seem…attainable.
Even funny.
That day I stopped pretending the healing.
We finally laugh together.

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard
passages.text:
I didn’t mean to laugh. 
It was polite. Sorta performative.
But the sound made her smile. 
And then she snorted.
I laughed again, for real this time.
We laughed until we cried.
I hadn’t laughed like that in years.
Now we are forever friends.
The fake laugh was just one thing.
But it changed everything

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard
passages.text:
It's contagious. And obnoxious.
A loud full-body experience.
Illegal in at least three counties.
She laughed once during prayer.
I collapsed.
Holy Spirit, or pure chaos?
Both.
We’ve healed with that laugh.
Sweated through shirts because of that laugh.
If you hear it, run toward it.
It's how you know you’re in the right room.



 





GROUP LAUGHTER IS A WEAPON


We meant to be serious.
But someone mispronounced “existential.”
Then someone snorted.
Followed by a fart.
We fell apart. All of us.
Sobriety in giggle form.
Nothing heals like laughing with people who’ve seen the real you.
Your messiest self is invited back again.
The meeting didn’t stay on topic.
But it saved us anyway.



 





HIT BY A BUS, BUT A FANCY ONE


It’s a Tuesday.
I’m tired.
Mascara is a concept, not a reality.
But I brush my hair.
Throw on lipstick.
Look in the mirror and mutter,
“You look like you got hit by a bus... 
but like, a charter bus. With climate control.”
Then I laugh. It’s shaky.
Because honestly?
That’s high praise in recovery.

 





THE PANTS WERE A LIE


They said “stretch denim.”
They lied.
I fought them like they were a moral enemy.
Collapsed onto the bed in defeat.
Mid-battle, I whispered,
“This is how we die. Bound by Levi’s. Unfulfilled.”
My dog looked concerned.
So did my thighs.
Eventually, I switched to leggings.
Because joy is elastic.
And Jesus? He wore robes.

 





THE BINDER WAS NOT A HOBBY


They laughed at my binder.
All those tabs.
Labeled: Goals. Budget. Emotional Spiral. Death.
But I wasn’t being quirky.
I was building a fortress.
Each divider, a weapon.
Each post-it, a psalm.
When life falls apart, I don’t crumble—I laminate.
You can’t fight chaos with vibes.
You need a Sharpie and a three-hole punch.


 





MY THERAPIST LAUGHED, SO I WON


I said something unusually awkward – but real.
She tried staying neutral.
She failed. Spectacularly.
We laughed for five full minutes.
Tears-in-eyes, can’t-breathe, therapist-lost-control laughter.
That’s how I knew I was getting better.
Not because I cried less.
But because I remembered what was hilarious.
Even broken.
Especially broken.
I should charge her for that session

alternates.note: Exact word-for-word duplicate of the 2025-05-09 passage (same six vignettes); nothing new.
alternates.text:
SIT IN THE WEIRD


I overthink.
Under-sleep.
And text you a paragraph with seven metaphors and a meme.
I say, “It’s not that deep.”
But it is.
It's also everything.
That’s how I’m built.
Cosmic and cracked.
Laughing at it all.
Sometimes crying between lines.
But listen.
Don’t try to fix me.
Just sit in the weird with me.
 





THE BUTTERNUT INCIDENT


I thought I bought a spaghetti squash.
But it was a butternut.
Carved into it with righteous fury.
It didn’t string. It splintered.
I was so grievously angry.
Nothing was peeling right for me.
So I hurled it at the compost bin.
Missed.
It rolled under my car.
Stayed there three weeks.
Same, butternut. Same.
 





HOPE COMES IN CHICKEN THIGHS


I don’t want lean protein.
You can have the chicken breasts.
Give me the thighs…
Brain-healing meat that tastes like a second chance.
Hope isn’t dry meat.
It's crispy skins and a side of buttered boundaries.
I fed myself well, finally.
Not with guilt.
With fuel for my soul.
Recovery is delicious.
Especially with mustard.
 





IF IT’S NOT FUNNY, IT’S NOT FINISHED


Here’s my rule:
If I can’t laugh yet, I’m not done healing.
It’ll come.
Like a punchline you didn’t see coming.
The moment grief turns ridiculous—
Holy ground.
Until then, I wait.
Plot.
Hold the silence.
Rehearse my joy in advance.
Polish the punchline.
Because when it flips?
Oh baby.
The laughter is freaking glorious.
 





FAST CAMEL ENERGY


I called it Fast Camel Mode.
Not because I was efficient—because I was frantic.
Dry humor, dry shampoo, and zero water.
Still I galloped forward, chaos trailing like toilet paper on my sandal.
But I’m learning now:
Even camels drink eventually.
And the ones who laugh while hauling baggage?
Those are the sacred beasts.
 





SUCH A HAPPY SNORT


She snorted in group once.
Ugly laugh. Real laugh.
It cracked my grief open.
I was still detoxing from all the pretending.
And she seemed so unfiltered.
Unapologetic even.
She made recovery seem…attainable.
Even funny.
That day I stopped pretending the healing.
We finally laugh together.
A sisterhood of snorters.
Because God is so good.

SUCH A HAPPY SNORT


She snorted in group once.
Ugly laugh. Real laugh.
It cracked my grief open.
I was still detoxing from all the pretending.
And she seemed so unfiltered.
Unapologetic even.
She made recovery seem…attainable.
Even funny.
That day I stopped pretending the healing.
We finally laugh together.
A sisterhood of snorters.
Because God is so good.








I VACUUMED A FROG


I didn’t see it.
Just heard the thunk.
Paused. Frozen.
Too late.
The frog was in the Dyson.
It haunted me.
Not because it died—because it lived.
Two days later it hopped out and judged me.
Wet. Dusty. Alive. Confused AF.
I felt that.
I named him Jerry.
I don’t think he forgave me.
 





OCD, OMC, COD... WHAT IS IT??? 


I alphabetize trauma.
List my fears.
Re-label them for fun.
OCD? Maybe.
OMC? (Oh My Chaos.)
COD? (Chronically Overwhelmed, Darling.)
Whatever it is, it’s all mine.
And it’s organized.
Usually color-coded.
Mental health isn’t always clinical.
Sometimes it’s just diagnosing yourself using acronym roulette.
And I’m okay with that.
Mostly.
Unless you move my Post-its.
 





HEAD SENSENESS


“I want someone who has head senseness,” I said.
They blinked.
I suppose I meant common sense.
Emotional regulation.
The ability to stay upright in crisis.
But “head senseness” felt more true.
It’s a vibe.
Rare.
You know it when you see it.
And you marry it when you’re lucky.
Or bribe it with lasagna.
 





ICEBERG POO


Someone said I was exaggerating.
I said, “I don’t just poo off the tip of an iceberg.”
Meaning: when I go, I go deep.
Barncle-deep. Echo-deep.
Don’t ask for surface-level drama and expect polite metaphors.
This isn’t Titanic Lite.
It’s Full Depth Emotional Release™, 
With weird grief-seahorses swimming laps around generational wounds.
Pack a snorkel.

chapters.title: New me
chapters.why: The small proofs of a changed woman: the text not answered, the sink cleaned instead of the bar, the haircut, and the Weasel laughed at instead of fought.
questions: The 2025-05-09 passage 'I Didn't Text Back': who sent the message with 'lies in bubbles,' and what did it say?
The 2025-05-09 passage 'I Cleaned the Sink': what was the bad day? What had happened that morning?
The 2025-09-15 passage 'The Recovery Haircut': when was this (still inside, sober house, later), and who is 'we'?

The 2025-05-09 passage 'I Chose Peace Over Proof' says you had receipts and didn't send them. Is this the same '252-page proof' from the 2026-06-06 passage? Who were you going to send them to, and what made you stop?
The 2025-09-15 passage 'The Weasel': 'I remade my henhouse' — what does that mean concretely? What did you rebuild after Becca?

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard
passages.text:
I saw the message.
It baited me.
Lies in bubbles.
Old me would’ve fought.
Typed too much.
Proved a point no one cared about.
Now?
I ignored it.
Ate a string cheese.
Sighed.
Put my phone down.
Let the silence be the answer.
Healing isn’t loud.
It’s just walking away without explaining a damn thing.







I BOUGHT A PLANT AND IT LIVED


I named her Consuela.
I watered her when I remembered.
Which, shockingly, was perfect.
She grew.
Not fast.
But green.
And when she bloomed?
So did something inside me.
Not because of the flower—because I was nurturing life.
Turns out, healing sometimes looks like soil under your nails.
And a cascade of leafy blooms.








I DIDN’T APOLOGIZE FOR EXISTING


I took up space in a meeting.
Said “no” without explaining.
Ate the last cookie.
Corrected someone out loud.
Wore bright lipstick to the grocery store.
For no reason.
And I didn’t shrink.
Didn’t apologize.
Didn’t make myself small to keep others comfortable.
That day?
I knew.
I can no longer be the old me.

 





I CLEANED THE SINK


It was a bad day.
So I washed the dishes first.
Old me would’ve stopped at the bar.
New me?
Needed the counter clear.
To create some order.
To start over.
To see I still had agency.
Healing looks like dish soap and grief.
One hand scrubbing.
The other letting go.
Both doing sacred work

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard - Finalizing
passages.text:
We chopped it off.
All of it.
Looked like a feral hedgehog or something.
But I grinned.
For the first time in a while, the outside matched the chaos within.
The world hated it.
But my soul whispered, “You’re free.”
Freedom looks like bad bangs and no regrets.
I tipped the stylist $20.
Bless her

passages.chat: ChatGPT · My Brain is Mustard - Finalizing
passages.text:
Weasels slink.
Smile.
Sanctify themselves with charm.
She was my friend.
Until she was my replacement.
Until she weaponized empathy like a ninja in yoga pants.
Until her lies bought her glory.
Eventually weasels expose their teeth.
Today, I laugh.
A rodent is always a rodent.
I remade my henhouse.
And the rooster still roosters
