alternates.text:
no.. they need to be grouped by what goes in each chapter not by which type of thing it is. here are the next ten.. please add in the things for each vignette as they are to appear, not grouped by type... 




NOT A BREAKDOWN—JUST A PIVOT


I wasn’t spiraling.
I was twirling.
Recalculating.
Getting new WiFi from heaven.
People thought, “She’s losing it.”
But I wasn’t.
I was loosening it.
Unclenching.
Unscheduling.
Untangling spaghetti thoughts from my miracle map.
You say breakdown.
I say reboot.
Also?
Shenanigans are also holy.
So is dancing barefoot during lunch.
On a Tuesday.
With pugs.





THE DAY I SAID NO 


One day, I said no. 
Full stop.
My old self would’ve explained.
Justified.
Sent an apology hot dish.
New me?
Said “No thanks,” and went to Target.
Didn’t spiral.
Didn’t backpedal.
Just said no.
A soft one.
A kind one.
Like a velvet sword.
Still sharp.
Still sacred.
Still swinging in the name of peace.






MUST BE THURSDAY AGAIN


The feeling hit.
The chaos.
The momentum.
The rich clarity.
And I thought, “Yep. Must be Thursday.”
Because that’s how I time-travel now.
In focus blocks.
Three hours of living fire.
Followed by twenty minutes of pug-walking dissociation.
Structure doesn’t kill creativity.
It cradles it gently.
Thursday is my sacred altar.
And I come prepared.

 





JESUS KNOWS I SWEAR SOMETIMES


I love the Lord.
And I say “ass” sometimes.
I’m not rebellious to offend - 
I’m rebellious because I’m honest.
He’s not threatened by my sass.
He laughed first, 
Because even heaven needs spice.
So yes, I pray with a side of sarcasm.
And sometimes Jesus answers with a wink.
Usually after a long pause.

 





WHISPERING THROUGH MASCARA


My prayers came choked.
Mascara-streaked.
Muttered in parking lots and bathroom stalls.
God didn’t mind.
He took the smeared confessions.
Made them holy.
I didn’t have to fold my hands.
Didn’t need a sanctuary.
Or music.
Or breath.
I just reached out and
He ran toward me.
Every time.
Even when I reeked of failure.

 
Squeeze Packs: Tangy Times
•	When someone underestimated you
•	A boss moment that needs to be remembered
•	Being dead wrong
•	What you didn’t say but should have
•	What you did say and wish you hadn’t
 





MY WORD’S BEEN THROUGH IT


Torn pages.
One coffee ring.
Sticky note with “WTF, LORD?” in all caps.
It’s held me together.
I’ve cried over it.
Wrestled it.
Ran away.
Came back.
It waited.
It's been a battle field.
It isn’t pristine.
Nor am I.
To say it’s ancient – is true. 
Mighty powerful too.
It's undone me more than once.






GRIEF MAKES YOU STUPID


I put deodorant on my toothbrush.
Twice.
Sat in the car wearing only one shoe.
I cried because the grapes were too round.
Grief rewires you.
Turns you into a punchline.
But you laugh because if you don’t, you dissolve.
So I laughed.
With snot.
With rage.
With gum in my hair.
It definitely counts.

 





THE FUNERAL FART


I didn’t mean to.
It was quiet. Reverent.
Until it wasn’t.
I bent over to hug Grandma and the sound escaped like a squeaky balloon at a baptism.
A small child laughed.
So did I.
Grief cracked open.
Laughter poured in.
I’m convinced heaven loves a good snort during sorrow.
God made butts, after all.



 





CRACKED PLATE THEOLOGY


I broke a plate when I sent him away.
Shattered it.
Kept the biggest piece.
I Sharpied, “Still useful” on it.
Because I am too.
It holds paper clips now.
Little things.
Like hope.
Redemption isn’t always stained glass.
Sometimes it’s duct-taped pottery and the reminder:
You don’t need to be whole to be holy.

 





THE RECOVERY HAIRCUT


We chopped it off.
All of it.
Looked like a feral hedgehog or something.
But I grinned.
For the first time in a while, the outside matched the chaos within.
The world hated it.
But my soul whispered, “You’re free.”
Freedom looks like bad bangs and no regrets.
I tipped the stylist $20.
Bless her.

alternates.text:
fix them from the last set I pasted AND STOP MAKING EVERYTHING SHORTER.. THE SPICY MUSTARD AND HONEY MUSTARD ARE SUPPOSED TO BE ALMOST A WHOLE PAGE OF JUCIY GOODNESS AND YOU'RE DOWN TO A SENTENCE.
 




NOT A BREAKDOWN—JUST A PIVOT


I wasn’t spiraling.
I was twirling.
Recalculating.
Getting new WiFi from heaven.
People thought, “She’s losing it.”
But I wasn’t.
I was loosening it.
Unclenching.
Unscheduling.
Untangling spaghetti thoughts from my miracle map.
You say breakdown.
I say reboot.
Also?
Shenanigans are also holy.
So is dancing barefoot during lunch.
On a Tuesday.
With pugs.





THE DAY I SAID NO 


One day, I said no. 
Full stop.
My old self would’ve explained.
Justified.
Sent an apology hot dish.
New me?
Said “No thanks,” and went to Target.
Didn’t spiral.
Didn’t backpedal.
Just said no.
A soft one.
A kind one.
Like a velvet sword.
Still sharp.
Still sacred.
Still swinging in the name of peace.






MUST BE THURSDAY AGAIN


The feeling hit.
The chaos.
The momentum.
The rich clarity.
And I thought, “Yep. Must be Thursday.”
Because that’s how I time-travel now.
In focus blocks.
Three hours of living fire.
Followed by twenty minutes of pug-walking dissociation.
Structure doesn’t kill creativity.
It cradles it gently.
Thursday is my sacred altar.
And I come prepared.

 





JESUS KNOWS I SWEAR SOMETIMES


I love the Lord.
And I say “ass” sometimes.
I’m not rebellious to offend - 
I’m rebellious because I’m honest.
He’s not threatened by my sass.
He laughed first, 
Because even heaven needs spice.
So yes, I pray with a side of sarcasm.
And sometimes Jesus answers with a wink.
Usually after a long pause.

 





WHISPERING THROUGH MASCARA


My prayers came choked.
Mascara-streaked.
Muttered in parking lots and bathroom stalls.
God didn’t mind.
He took the smeared confessions.
Made them holy.
I didn’t have to fold my hands.
Didn’t need a sanctuary.
Or music.
Or breath.
I just reached out and
He ran toward me.
Every time.
Even when I reeked of failure.

chapters.title: Standing in it without flinching
chapters.why: The long tail of recovery: off the meds, no cravings, four years relearning how to feel, the therapist who sees through the entertainment.
questions: What medication were you put on at Teen Challenge, what did surrendering to it feel like the first day, and how did you and Vicky Dean discover you'd stopped? Was it a decision or did you just forget?
What did you answer Vicky Dean when she asked what grounds you? Say it the way you said it to her.

The 2025-10-08 passage says you've spent four years learning to present emotionally healthy. Give one specific moment where you had to think hard about how to react (a funeral, a friend's news) and what you did.
'i made eye contact with a feeling and lived' — which feeling, and where were you?
The 2026-05-12 passage says you were arrested four times in two years and now never think about drinking. When was the last time you were in a liquor store parking lot, and what happened?

passages.chat: Stopping unwanted Christmas music in car
passages.text: I mean, it has because I feel like I was talking to Vicky Dean yesterday. Vicky Dean is my, like, mental health lady. She's the one that has been, like, since I was at Teen Challenge, she's been the prescriber. And yesterday, we realized that I have not taken any medication for mental health purposes for over a year, and I haven't even thought about it. Like, it was... I I didn't never wanna take medicine, but when I went there, I surrendered to it all, and I surrendered to, okay, if they would... if they think this is good. And so I took medication for probably two and a half or three years, but I haven't taken anything for a year and a half now. Probably a year and a half. So I was really excited about that actually. But, anyway, she said yesterday that, we... she asked me this question. It was such a good question too. She said, what is it about you? because she said that she uses my journey when she talks to other people because my journey has been so thoughtful and, you know, she... and so she said to me, what is it that grounds you specifically? Is it words? And I had to think about it because think about how I use words like writing and whatever, but I don't think it is the words. I think what it is is the building of these systems and stuff like that because I feel like when I'm building these systems, it frees up my spirit to heal from stuff. And so I feel like, you know, since my mom and Chuck died, my dog Chuck died, I feel like I've been on this quest to just find, like, peace because I haven't been writing as much, and I've... but I've been building stuff, like, flow suite and whatever. There's something that happens when I'm creating that kind of order for people that is so important to my mental health because it's... and I suppose maybe it's a habit because all the way along, like, when I was working for my dad, and that was so emotionally stressful and stuff like that, like, I did it then to, like, I used to build systems or clean up stuff or make a new idea about something. But I don't I don't... I feel like that is my healing space. Like, when I'm doing it, it frees up the angst and the anxiety and the horror of some of the stuff. Sometimes the traumas and stuff like that. I feel like it's my healthy way of sinking into something that frees up my spirit to heal.

passages.chat: Claude · Writing about the life I didn't live
passages.text:
Yeah. Exactly. It's really good to realize two things right now. And number one is that... so it says in scripture that all things all things work together for the good of those who love the Lord. And I think that when you look at my life, that that's very, very evident that because I was obedient to the Lord and what the Lord was telling me to do, I think it took God some really bold things. I think that's why I've had my DWIs. I I was caught every time I drink. Like, I wasn't drinking solid for those two years, but every time I drink in those two years, I got arrested four times. I got arrested. four times I drink. I, you know, I think God had his hand in them. And I I wonder too, like, with the conviction that recovery has been so easy for me. Like, not the recovery itself, not going through all the things that I had to go through emotionally and the team challenge year and all the things that chasing chickens is about. They weren't easy, but sobriety is easy for me. I don't ever think about drinking or want to go back to that. It never comes up on my radar. And there was literally times when I'd be driving, and I was trying to be sober or whatever. And I would... I couldn't stop driving into a liquor store parking lot. If I saw one, I drove in and I bought liquor. Like, it... I don't I don't understand how that was my life at one point, and now I'm so free of it without the notion that at some level that God... it took that for God to give me to pay attention to what God wanted for me. And so in a way, I'm grateful for my alcoholism or that experience in my life because I think it was my ticket to freedom.



---

passages.chat: Stopping unwanted Christmas music in car
passages.text: When there's one more story, I wanna pop in here too because this matters too. The other day, I took my brother to meet with somebody to help him navigate through some stuff. He's he's only been out of prison for six months now. He had it on February, something like that. Six months. Almost exactly six months. And, he's having trouble and rightly so. Like, my brother's never been good with money. He's always been given handouts. He's always been given too much, blah blah blah. And so I'm trying to navigate through all this right now is challenging. He's doing a really good job. Anyway, so after we got done at the session... okay. This is so funny actually because he texted me, and he said, I was just telling my friend here at the house that he lives at, that there's something so calming about your presence that when you're with me, I can actually learn what other people are trying to teach me. Isn't that beautiful? But also hilarious because when Scott woke up from being shot, like, I was trying to... this was in August of twenty twenty one, which was, you know, basically two months before I got sober myself. And he was like, am I... is this heaven? because he never thought he'd ever see his whole family again together. And my brother really loves his family, but he was so separate. Like, he really was... I didn't talk to my brother at one point for twelve years. And so, anyway, so when he woke up, I was trying to get him to suck on this thing because he needed some moisture in his mouth, and, he couldn't have any water or anything because he was gonna go in surgery again. movements.name: The Porch
movements.note: This movement holds the life you built after the program: the jobs you took, the two weddings that didn't happen, the granddaughters, your dad coming back through the door at Athena's party, your mom's death, Scott's release, the Mother's Day brunch at Joe and Becca's, the return to the Catholic church, and the five-year date on October 1. The spine is the people coming back to you — Adam, your dad, Scott, your sister, Nicole reaching out — set against the one wound that hasn't closed (Becca, and the boys' life with her). The strongest material is the scenes: the lemon swab and 'still so bossy,' your dad walking back in, the staff lining the hallway for your mom, Nicole sobbing on speakerphone. What's thin is the everyday porch itself — where you live now, what a Tuesday with Athena looks like, and the actual voices of Adam and Jakob in the present; most of the family material is told about them, not with them.
bigQuestions: There is no scene anywhere in this movement of Jakob and you together in the present — no hug, no words from him about getting his mom back. If Jakob has ever said something like that to you, when and where was it, and what were his exact words?

The reader never sees the porch. Where do you live now (the 2026-08-09 passage mentions driving past the Stone Arch Bridge daily), what does the place look like, and what does an ordinary morning there hold?

Several passages (the 2026-01-14 passage, the 2026-05-12 passage, the 2026-08-05 passage) circle the question of leaving Minnesota — Tennessee with Pete, Florida where Marley and your dad are. Have you decided, in words, that you are staying in Minnesota for the grandchildren? When did you say it out loud and to whom?

Adam has almost no present-day voice in this movement — he calls once in the 2026-01-14 passage and hands you a baby on Tuesdays. Is there one recent conversation with Adam, in his words, about what these five years have been like from his side?

The movement needs its own one-line summary from you — the difference between getting sober and getting free. the 2026-05-12 passage says alcoholism was your 'ticket to freedom' and the 2026-08-05 passage says 'my life is freedom right now.' Is there a single moment when you first said that sentence out loud, and to whom?

chapters.title: Every Reasonable Job
chapters.why: The movement opens where the program ended — the first paycheck, the probation letter, the slow climb off public support that makes everything after it possible.
questions: The 2025-09-29 passage says you took a job collecting urine for drug testing and then 'every reasonable job' after it. What was the first day of the urine job like — who hired you, what did you tell them about yourself, and what was the next job after that one?

The 2025-05-03 passage says Wright County probation ends July 27, 2025 and Hennepin needs $107,000 in restitution first. What happened on July 27 — did the letter come, did you do anything to mark it — and where does the Hennepin restitution stand today?
The 2025-09-29 passage says you got off all public support including health insurance. Do you remember the day you cancelled it or the letter that came — what that moment actually looked like?

passages.text:
ok..we're doing something different.. lol i'm going to try pasting them five at a time and we're going to do all the "extra" s at once before i paste them into the "book"

here are the next five.. don't forget to mix it up.. we don't want to be stale:






THE 13TH CLUCK

13 is not unlucky. It’s undeniable.
Adam born: 11.13.91.
Emily born: 11.13.92.
Jakob born: 2.13.95.
Nicole married Jakob: 5.13.22.
God loves a baker’s dozen, no?
Twelve disciples—and Jesus.
Twelve tribes—and God.
Thirteen is divine math.
It’s the bonus, the blessing, the proof.
This number follows me.
Not superstition—
just a lovely sacred sequence.

 





FIRST VIEW


I thought my heart was already as big as it could be.
Then came these tiny girls who each look like their daddies…
And the whole universe cracked open.
It wasn’t a second chance.
It's a whole new world.
A softness I didn’t know I needed.
I fell in. And I haven’t climbed out since.
 





SIT IN THE WEIRD


I overthink.
Under-sleep.
And text you a paragraph with seven metaphors and a meme.
I say, “It’s not that deep.”
But it is.
It's also everything.
That’s how I’m built.
Cosmic and cracked.
Laughing at it all.
Sometimes crying between lines.
But listen.
Don’t try to fix me.
Just sit in the weird with me.
 





HOPE CHICKEN THIGHS


I don’t want lean protein.
You can have the chicken breasts.
Give me the thighs…
Brain-healing meat that tastes like a second chance.
Hope isn’t dry meat.
It's crispy skins and a side of buttered boundaries.
I fed myself well, finally.
Not with guilt.
With fuel for my soul.
Recovery is delicious.
Especially with mustard.
 





IF IT’S NOT FUNNY, IT’S NOT FINISHED


Here’s my rule:
If I can’t laugh yet, I’m not done healing.
It’ll come.
Like a punchline you didn’t see coming.
The moment grief turns ridiculous—
Holy ground.
Until then, I wait.
Plot.
Hold the silence.
Rehearse my joy in advance.
Polish the punchline.
Because when it flips?
Oh baby.
The laughter is freaking glorious.

passages.chat: Claude · Finding the Chasing Chickens chapter outline
passages.text: Oh my gosh. Okay. So I I think I got married. I think I so I chose Joe because I believe that he did what he said he was gonna do. And at that age, he did. And so he was really, like, a solid person in my life. And so we got married when we met when I was, in my teens. We got married when I was 21. So we were together for 5 years before we got married. And We had I We got married in January 5, 2020 or 1991, and then I was pregnant with Adam by March 12, 2020. 1991. And I was immediately ill. I had to be in the hospital that Memorial Day weekend. I I remember that specifically and other other points. On day 12, like, at first, it was emergency room visits, and then it was hospitalization. And then I eventually went home with IVs. passages.text:
let's try this.. 

and i want to know if it has the same resonance as the other two do

Faith and Diet Coke
There are so many things that accompany the death of a parent. Practical things. Moving things. Business-as-usual things.
Then there are the spiritual things.
And in my deep, abiding faith—the faith that saved me, the faith that brought me back from the deep end, the faith I have staked my whole life on—I still have questions.
What's happening to her right now? Is she cold? Is she okay? Does she have her Diet Coke?
That last one might sound ridiculous. But if you knew my mother, you'd know it's not. Diet Coke was her thing in her last months. Her constant. Her comfort. And I can't stop wondering if somehow, wherever she is, she has one.
I believe in heaven. I believe the Lord caught her the moment she left. I believe she is free from the striving and the confusion and the pain of a body and a brain that stopped working the way they should.
I believe all of that.
And I still want to know if she's cold.
—
I don’t think I’m having a failure of faith. Maybe it’s just love. Because love almost always asks questions that theology can't answer. Love wonders about Diet Coke and being warm and whether those involved are being kind to her body.
I think sometimes we expect faith to wrap everything up neatly—to hand us peace like a package with a bow on it. But that's not how it works. At least not for me. Not today.
Today, faith looks like believing she's with Jesus and still hoping someone thought to bring a warm, fuzzy blanket AND a soft pink sweatshirt.
Today, faith looks like trusting the Lord is fighting for me while I sit here wondering what happens next, about what life looks like when such a big tiny person is no longer here.
Today, faith looks like questions I can't answer and peace I can't explain, both living in the same breath.
—
The Lord will fight for you; you need only be still.
So.
I'm being still. I'm letting the questions come. I'm not running from them or numbing them or pretending I have it all figured out.
Because the other thing I know is that acceptance is enough for today. Whether you have a Diet Coke or not.

The 2026-05-12 passage says you were arrested every one of the four times you drank in those two years. Is that four DWIs, or four arrests of different kinds — and which one is the Hennepin County case in the 2025-05-03 passage?

passages.chat: Sobriety date as recovery capital
passages.text:
tell me where to chante things because you weren't working the original 
What I’ve Been Doing (An Accounting)
You know how some people go quiet because nothing’s happening?
That’s not what this was.
I’ve been quiet the way a workshop is quiet from the street. Which is to say: not quiet at all, you just couldn’t hear it from where you were standing. Come closer. Smell the sawdust.
Here’s the accounting, because I keep books for a living and I might as well keep this one in public.
I built software. Actual software, with my own hands — a whole suite of business tools, the kind of thing you’re supposed to need a department for. I had a keyboard, a stubborn streak, and an unreasonable amount of Diet Dr Pepper, and it turns out that’s a department.
I launched a book. A women’s ministry book — out in the world now, doing its work without me hovering, which is the whole point of launching things.
I edited a book of poetry — a friends collection of her mother’s words. It’s a real legacy, held steady between covers. The daughter and I played music together for decades and she used to sigh when I said let’s run that part one more time. It’s ironic that now I was able to give her mother’s voice a “one more time” experience. I print my own things, so I know exactly what it costs to put a life between covers. It was an honor to help carry this one. And also, it fed my spirit a little when the work made my friend a little weepy.
I’m finishing my own memoir. It’s called Chasing Chickens, it comes out October 28, and it required me to go back through every room of my life with a flashlight and a legal pad. Some rooms I had to visit twice. One or three I had to visit with backup.
And, honestly, I grieved. That’s on the ledger too, because an honest accounting doesn’t skip the hard columns. There were moments this season when the only thing holding me upright was the systems I’d already built — the routines, the structures, the load-bearing habits that keep working on the days you can’t. I think that’s why I build them. Not for the good weeks. For those moments.
Definitely not least, I’ve been spending a great deal of time being Grandma Kiki. That one goes in the ledger too — the hours with my granddaughters that nobody invoices, because some assets are too valuable to bill. Ask any bookkeeper which entries actually hold the books together. It’s never the ones with dollar signs.
Listen, reader.
Next month, on October 1, my sobriety turns five years old. Which is the line item under all the other line items. None of the rest of this ledger exists without it. That’s not me being sentimental — that’s me being an accurate Keeper.
The Preacher said it plainly: “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might” (Ecclesiastes 9:10, ESV). Not halfway. Not someday. The work in front of your hands, done with gusto, excellence, and grit — that’s the whole assignment, and this season I did it with all three.
But here’s what I’ve learned about seasons like this one: building and writing use the same hands, and the hands were busy. I wasn’t blocked. I wasn’t empty. I was load-bearing — and there’s a difference between a writer who’s stopped and a writer who’s carrying drywall.
The drywall is up now. The workshop made its things.
Oh — and full disclosure, because an accounting is supposed to list all assets: somewhere in this season I acquired an alter ego. She’s called The Keeper. Cape optional, clipboard mandatory, saves things instead of chasing them. Every superhero gets an origin story, and mine, apparently, involved a lot of chickens.

So I’m coming back to the desk — back to The 13th Room, my little corner for the spiritually gifted and structurally inconvenient. A new series starts September 10: thirteen posts, because of course it’s thirteen, walking us all the way to launch day. And there’s a zine on the workbench called Stop It, which is exactly what it sounds like and none of what you expect.
That’s what I’ve been doing.
Now watch what I do next.
Go sparkle!

passages.chat: Claude · Writing about the life I didn't live
passages.text:
Yeah. Exactly. It's really good to realize two things right now. And number one is that... so it says in scripture that all things all things work together for the good of those who love the Lord. And I think that when you look at my life, that that's very, very evident that because I was obedient to the Lord and what the Lord was telling me to do, I think it took God some really bold things. I think that's why I've had my DWIs. I I was caught every time I drink. Like, I wasn't drinking solid for those two years, but every time I drink in those two years, I got arrested four times. I got arrested. four times I drink. I, you know, I think God had his hand in them. And I I wonder too, like, with the conviction that recovery has been so easy for me. Like, not the recovery itself, not going through all the things that I had to go through emotionally and the team challenge year and all the things that chasing chickens is about. They weren't easy, but sobriety is easy for me. I don't ever think about drinking or want to go back to that. It never comes up on my radar. And there was literally times when I'd be driving, and I was trying to be sober or whatever. And I would... I couldn't stop driving into a liquor store parking lot. If I saw one, I drove in and I bought liquor. Like, it... I don't I don't understand how that was my life at one point, and now I'm so free of it without the notion that at some level that God... it took that for God to give me to pay attention to what God wanted for me. And so in a way, I'm grateful for my alcoholism or that experience in my life because I think it was my ticket to freedom.

passages.chat: Faith Recovery Interview Questions  *(updated 2026-08-29, 490 of your words)*
passages.text:
I have not had one craving. Which is amazing considering how I thought I couldn’t survive if I didn’t have my doc at hand at all times. It consumed my focus and energy. 

I did have consequences and setbacks and guilt. I worked through each one the same way I survived 366 days at teen challenge - literally uber focused on the next right choice - one at a time and then the next. 

I have no fear. And for someone who lived with the unending fear of disappointing those who depended on me for things, being fearless is marvelous. It’s what comes from knowing who’s you are and who you are

passages.chat: Sobriety date as recovery capital
passages.text:
Your date is up to you. There are no esoteric rules to obey. 

However. 

When I wasn’t committed to my date - I also wasn’t in sobriety yet. I know that only by knowing what actual sobriety feels like. 

Now that I have a date and am thrilled about it aging into five years (!!!!) on October 1, it’s become part of my recovery capital. If I were to even THINK of taking another drink, I know it would pop in my mind that I don’t want to change my date. And a single drink would make it impossible for me to keep my date because it would not feel true to me. 

So. Examine your thoughts and check your side of the street. Why are you okay with keeping a sober date if it’s not your actual sober date. If your reasons are purely pure, keep your date. If there are things hiding in there, let this be a warning to you to GET HELP NOW!!!!
